profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:13.456+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

Later on, a scholar at Tiāntái
Cao defeated Yuán Shàng,

and subsequently resided in Yè.
Yè,
the administrative center of Hàn's Wèi Commandery.
Wèi,
a grand name;
he was thus conferred the title of Duke of Wèi.
A prophecy also said:
"The one to replace Hàn will be exalted."
The exalted one,

Emperor Wéndì received the abdication of Hàn,

The supreme ancestor, Emperor Wén,
personal name Pī,
styled Zǐhuán,
was the eldest son of King Cāo.
The posthumous title rules: diligent in learning and fond of questioning is called Wén.
Supreme ancestor,

According to ritual,
the ancestor has merit and the progenitor has virtue.
The posthumous title rule: with widespread influence reflecting in all directions is called supreme;
receiving the mandate without changing is called supreme.
Bringing peace to the people through rules is called emperor;
clear in a single virtue is called emperor;
clear in uniting with the Dao is called emperor.
With virtues resembling heaven and earth is called emperor;
acting in accordance with Dao without doing is called emperor.
In the first year of Huángchū
(Gēngzǐ, 220), Wèi received Hàn's abdication,
advancing the cycle of the Five Virtues,
continuing earth after fire.
The color of earth is yellow,

In October of that year, when he received the abdication,

Spring,

King Wǔ arrived in Luòyáng;
Gēngzǐ,
he passed away.
King of Wèi, Cao was posthumously titled Wǔ.
Difficult to dazzle with deception.
Dazzled refers to
eyes having no consistent master;
difficult to dazzle with deception,

Not restricting the lowly,
employing talents according to their abilities,

When facing enemies in formation,

For meritorious accomplishments deserving reward,

without merit, expecting reward,

He did not separate the talented and influential.
The talented,

If someone committed a crime, punishment was certain,

Habitually restrained and economical,

Therefore, he was able to cut down the unruly,

"Nearly"
here,

To cut down,

Nearly,

the troops were agitated.

The soldiers from Qīngzhōu

Qīngzhōu soldiers,

Jiǎ Kuí said:

Xián explains: the old city of Wū is north of present Kuízhoū Wū Shān County.
Dù Yòu says: Wū,
is Bādōng County of Guīzhōu.
He also states: Wū Shān County,
is the Wū Prefecture of Chǔ;
under Hàn, it was Wū County,
the old city lies north of present county,
Jìn established Jiànpíng County here.
Over forty thousand troops.
The Wǔlíng tribes all sent envoys to seek troops,
Quán appointed Lù Xùn as Grand Commander, and temporarily Commander-in-Chief,
to lead generals Zhū Rán, Pān Zhāng, Sòng Qiān, Hán Dāng, Xú Shèng, Xiānyú Dān, Sūn Huán, and others, fifty thousand to resist them.
Sūn Quán initially appointed Lǚ Mèng as Grand Commander to take Guān Yǔ,
now re-appoints Lù Xùn as Grand Commander to resist Liú Bèi.
The title of Grand Commander likely began here.

Emperor's younger brothers, Yānlíng Marquis Zhāng, Wǎn Marquis Jù, Lǔyáng Marquis Yǔ, Qiáo Marquis Lín, Zàn Marquis Gǔn, Xiāngyì Marquis Jùn, Hóngnóng Marquis Gàn, Shòuchūn Marquis Biāo, Lìchéng Marquis Huī, and Píngyú Marquis Mào were all elevated to Duke;
Ānxiāng Marquis Zhí was re-titled Zhēnchéng Marquis.
Zhí had been demoted due to suspicion,
now elevated to County Marquis.
Zhēnchéng belongs to Dōng County.
In Shǔ's records, it is written as
"Juànchéng,"
which should be followed.
Juàn,
pronounced juàn.
The Cloud Terrace was constructed at the tomb.
According to the River Classic Commentary,
the Cloud Terrace was within Luòyáng city,
east of the Gold Market.
At first,
the Emperor ordered the secretaries to speculate whether Liú Bèi would avenge Guān Yǔ on Sūn Quán,
and all agreed:
"Shǔ is a small state,
its only famous general was Yǔ;
upon Yǔ's death and the army's defeat,
fear and anxiety permeate within the borders,
they have no reason to mobilize again."
Courtier Liú Yè alone stated:
"Though Shǔ is small and weak,
small,
equivalent to narrow.
They must use their forces to show strength.
Besides, Guān Yǔ and Bèi,
had a bond as ruler and minister,
affection as if father and son;
if Guān Yǔ died,
and they did not mobilize an army to avenge him,
it would not fulfill their start-to-end duty."
In the eighth month,
Sūn Quán sent envoys proclaiming himself a vassal,
humbly submitting,
and sent back Yú Jìn and others.
Quán's conquest of Nánjùn involved capturing Yú Jìn,
described in the previous volume of the Reign of Ling Emperor, Jiàn'ān Year Twenty-Four.
Liú Yè alone said:
"Quán seeks surrender without reason,
there must be pressing matters within.
Quán previously assaulted and killed Guān Yǔ,
prompting Liú Bèi to surely launch a major campaign against him.
With strong external foes,
internal anxiety spread,
he fears Zhōngguó might take advantage of the situation,
hence he seeks surrender,
first to repulse Zhōngguó's troops,
second to leverage Zhōngguó's aid,
to fortify his populace and deceive enemies.
Liú Yè's insights,
precisely capture Quán's cunning intent.
Zhōngguó holds nine-tenths of power,
Wú and Shǔ each guard a prefecture,
to speak broadly,
it meant Wú guards Yáng,
Shǔ guards Yì.
When urgency arises, they aid each other,
this is the advantage of small states;
now, returning to attack each other,
Heaven forsakes them,
thus it's fitting to raise a large army,
cross the river directly to attack.
Shǔ attacks externally,
while we strike internally,
Wú's demise would not surpass ten days.
Wú's fall would leave Shǔ isolated,
if we split half of Wú with Shǔ,
Shǔ could not survive long,
not to mention Shǔ gains the exterior,
and we obtain the interior!"
The Emperor said:
"If we attack after their declaration of submission,
it would raise suspicions among those who might submit.
Better to accept Wú's submission first and then attack Shǔ later."
He replied:
"Shǔ is distant while Wú is near,
upon hearing Zhōngguó's attack,
they would retreat their troops,
and can't be stopped.
Now Bèi is already angry,
launching troops against Wú,
upon hearing of our attack on Wú,
knowing Wú's impending fall,
he would joyously proceed to compete with us for Wú's lands,
not change plans or restrain his anger to aid Wú."
Restrain,
to stop.
Thus Wú's submission was accepted.
If Wèi had followed Liú Yè's advice,
Wú would have been in great danger.
Yú Jìn’s hair and beard were white as snow,
his appearance haggard and worn.
When he saw the Emperor,
he wept, kowtowed, and bowed his head to the ground.
The Emperor consoled him with the stories of Xún Línfù and Mèng Míngshì.
The Jin minister Xún Línfù fought against Chu,
was defeated at Bì,
but Duke Jǐng of Jin reinstated him and used him to conquer the Red Dí.
The Qin minister Mèng Míng was captured by Jin at Xiáo,
but Duke Mù of Qin reinstated him and used him to dominate the Western Róng.
Fù
is pronounced fǔ.
The title General Who Pacifies the Distant Lands
was also unprecedented before this.
The Emperor had Yú Jìn go to the tomb chamber and view paintings depicting Guān Yǔ’s victories, Páng Dé’s fury, and Yú Jìn’s surrender and submission.
Huà
is interchangeable with the ancient character for painting.
Yú Jìn died from shame and resentment.
Your subject Guāng comments: Yú Jìn commanded tens of thousands of troops,
yet when defeated, he did not choose death
but surrendered alive to the enemy.
Later, he returned;
Emperor Wén could have dismissed him,
or executed him.
Yet he had paintings made in the tomb chamber to humiliate him—
this was unworthy of a ruler!
Rewarding the good and punishing the wicked is what defines a ruler.
On the 16th day, Dīngsì,
the Emperor dispatched the Minister of Ceremonies Xíng Zhēn to present the edict and appoint Sūn Quán as King of Wú,
granting him the Nine Bestowments.
Jí
means “to go to.”
“This should not be done.
The late Emperor campaigned across the world,
conquering eight-tenths of it,
and his might shook all within the seas.
Your Majesty received the abdication and assumed the true throne,
your virtue matches Heaven and Earth,
and your reputation reaches the four distant corners.
Although Sūn Quán has outstanding talent,
he is merely the former Han General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Nánchāng—
the titles General of Agile Cavalry and Marquis of Nánchāng
were conferred by Cáo Cāo while controlling the Han court,
as recorded in the previous volume, in the 24th year of the Jiàn’ān era of Han.
The officials and people of Wú still fear the Central Plains.
We should not force them into completing their schemes.
If we have no choice but to accept their surrender,
we may advance his general title
and enfeoff him as a marquis with a hundred thousand households,
but we should not immediately make him a king.
The rank of king is only one step below the Son of Heaven,
and their rituals, ranks, carriages, and attire would become confused.
Since the reigns of Emperors Jǐng and Wǔ of Han,
the feudal kings have been curtailed,
not allowed to share the same institutions as the capital.
Ever since Cáo Cāo became King of Wèi
and received the Nine Bestowments,
the rituals, ranks, carriages, and attire have been confused with those of the Son of Heaven.
The officials and people south of the Yangtze have no sense of allegiance as ruler and subject.
If we trust their false surrender
and proceed to enfeoff and nurture them—
fēng
means to grant land to cultivate them.
Zhí
means to nurture them to flourish.
Once their ruler-subject relationship is established,
it would be like adding wings to a tiger.
Once Sūn Quán receives the kingship,
after repelling the Shǔ army,
outwardly he will show full courtesy in serving the Central Plains,
making sure all within his state hear of it,
while inwardly acting without propriety to provoke Your Majesty’s anger.
When Your Majesty blazes with anger
and raises troops to chastise him,
he will then leisurely tell his people:
‘I devoted myself to serving the Central Plains,
sparing no treasures or valuables,
presenting tribute according to the seasons,
not daring to neglect the rites of a subject.
Yet they attack me without cause,
determined to destroy my state
and capture my people to serve as slaves and concubines.’
The people of Wú would have no reason not to believe his words.
Believing him, they would be stirred to anger,
and with ruler and subjects united in heart,
their combat strength would increase tenfold.”
Again, the Emperor did not listen.
The historian notes that the Emperor twice ignored Liú Yè’s advice,
setting the stage for the later failed campaign against Wú.
The general sentiment was lax and relaxed,
only the General Who Conquers the South, Xiàhóu Shàng, intensified preparations for offense and defense.
Cáo Wěi of Shānyáng,
long renowned for his talent—
this refers to Shānyáng Commandery,
belonging to Yǎnzhōu—
as a commoner, exchanged letters with the King of Wú seeking bribes,
hoping to establish connections in the capital.
The Emperor, hearing of this, executed him.
17. Wú also fortified Wǔchāng.
Having already fortified Shítóu,
they now fortified Wǔchāng—
this was the foundation of Wú’s defense of the Yangtze.
18. Earlier,
the Emperor intended to appoint Yáng Biāo as Grand Commandant.
Yáng Biāo declined, saying:
“I once served as one of the Three Excellencies of the Han court.
Encountering an age of decline and chaos,
I could not achieve the slightest benefit.
If I were to become a minister of Wèi,
for the state’s selection,
it would bring no honor either.”
The Emperor then desisted.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐhài,
the dukes and ministers held court at the new moon morning,
and Yáng Biāo was also invited,
treated with the etiquette due a guest.
He was bestowed a longevity staff—
The Odes says: “Its chēng and its jū.”
The commentary says: Jū
is guì.
Sūn Yán says: Guì
has swollen joints,
suitable for making staffs.
Lù Jī’s annotation says: The joints are swollen,
used to support the aged.
Nowadays, people use it for horsewhips and staffs.
Hóngnóng and the northern mountains have plenty of it.
Lù says: This is what is now called the língshòu staff.
Yán Shígǔ says: The wood resembles bamboo,
with branches and joints,
no longer than eight or nine chǐ,
three or four cùn in circumference,
naturally conforming to staff standards,
requiring no carving or shaping.
Chén Cángqì says: It grows in the valleys of Jiànnán,
round and long with purple bark.
Made into a staff,
it prolongs life and increases longevity.
He was made to wear a plain cloth robe and a leather cap for the audience;
appointed as Grandee of the Palace,
with a salary of two thousand dàn—
Under Han institutions, the Grandee of the Palace was ranked at two thousand dàn.
The Jìn Treatise says: The Grandee of the Palace,
established in Han times,
had no fixed number of positions.
It was often used for envoys granting temporary titles, bestowing funeral gifts, or overseeing funerals.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
it became increasingly esteemed,
no longer used as an envoy position.
When various dukes retired due to age,
they were granted this rank at home;
and for prominent officials at court,
it was additionally conferred.
Its rank was just below the Three Excellencies.
He was also permitted to have hitching posts at his gate—
Under Wèi and Jìn institutions,
the Three Excellencies and those with equivalent rank
had hitching posts at their gates.
Chéng Dàchāng says: Hitching posts consist of
one horizontal beam in the middle,
with two beams crossing through it,
placed at the four corners,
set up at the gate
to serve as a barrier and restriction.
The Rites of Zhōu calls them bìhù,
which are the forked barriers in front of government offices today.
All this was to honor and exalt him.
He died at the age of eighty-four.
Yáng Biāo fell far short of Gǒng Shèng.
19. Due to high grain prices,
the five-zhū coin was abolished.
The five-zhū coin had been reinstated not long before, only to be abolished again.
In the 20th year, the Lúshuǐ Hú under Zhì Yuánduō and others rebelled,
causing great turmoil west of the Yellow River.
The Emperor recalled Zōu Qí,
appointing the Capital Region Governor Zhāng Jì as Governor of Liáng Province,
and sending the Protector of the Army Xiàhóu Rú, General Fèi Yào, and others to follow him.
Over 7,000 Hú cavalrymen intercepted Zhāng Jì at Zhān Yīn Pass.
Zhān Yīn County
belonged to Āndìng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
and to Wǔwēi Commandery in the Later Hàn.
Zhān Yīn Pass
was the mouth of the Zhān Yīn River.
(Zhāng Jì) then secretly advanced via Qiěcì to reach Wǔwēi.
According to the records of both Hàn dynasties,
Wǔwēi had a Xūcì County.
Mèng Kāng said: Xū
is pronounced zǐ rú fān.
Cì
is pronounced zī.
This is Qiěcì.
(He) then withdrew to Xiǎnměi.
Xiǎnměi County
belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery in the Former Hàn;
it belonged to Wǔwēi Commandery in the Later Hàn as well as during Wèi and Jìn.
By then, Fèi Yào had arrived,
but Xiàhóu Rú and others had not yet reached him.
Zhāng Jì rewarded and feasted his officers and men,
intending to advance and attack the Hú.
All his generals said:
"The soldiers are weary,
and the enemy's morale is high.
It is difficult to confront them directly."
Zhāng Jì said:
"Now our army has no immediate grain supplies;
we must rely on the enemy for provisions.
If the enemy sees our forces united,
they will retreat deep into the mountains.
Pursuing them would mean traversing dangerous paths and facing starvation,
but if we withdraw our troops, they will emerge to raid and plunder.
In such a situation,
the military conflict cannot be resolved.
This is the so-called 'releasing the enemy for a single day,
brings calamity for generations to come.'"
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records
Xiān Zhěn saying:
"Releasing the enemy for a single day,
brings calamity for generations to come."
In the eleventh month,
several thousand Hú cavalrymen
took advantage of a strong wind to set fire to the camp,
causing great fear among the officers and men.
Zhāng Jì secretly hid 3,000 elite troops in ambush at night,
sending his Army Advisor Chénggōng Yīng to lead over a thousand cavalry in a feigned attack.
The Surname Register states: The descendants of Duke Chéng of Wèi took Chénggōng as their surname.
I dare not claim this is reliable.
The Hú indeed rushed to engage them,
whereupon the ambush was sprung, cutting off their retreat.
Attacking from front and rear,
(Zhāng Jì's forces) inflicted a major defeat,
beheading and capturing tens of thousands.
The region west of the Yellow River was completely pacified.
Later, Qū Guāng of Xīpíng rebelled,
killing the commandery governor.
The generals wanted to attack him,
but Zhāng Jì said:
"Only Qū Guāng and his followers are rebelling;
the people of the commandery are not necessarily all in agreement.
If we immediately bring the army against them,
the officials, commoners, Qiāng, and Hú will surely think the state cannot distinguish right from wrong,
and this will cause them all to cling together.
This would be like adding wings to a tiger.
Qū Guāng and his followers wish to use the Qiāng and Hú as support.
Now, first have the Qiāng and Hú raid and attack them,
offering generous rewards for recruitment.
All captives and spoils
shall be given to them.
This will externally thwart their momentum,
and internally disrupt their alliances.
It will surely be settled without battle."
He then issued a proclamation to inform the various Qiāng tribes,
pardoning those who had been misled by Qū Guāng and others;
those who could behead the rebel leaders and deliver their heads would be rewarded with titles and gifts.
Thereupon, Qū Guāng's followers beheaded him and sent his head,
and the rest remained peaceful as before.
21 Xíng Zhēn arrived in Wú.
The people of Wú believed he should be addressed as Supreme General,
Lord of the Nine Provinces.
According to the royal system for the Nine Provinces,
one province was the domain of the Son of Heaven,
and the eight other provinces had eight lords.
The King of Wú said:
"Lord of the Nine Provinces
is something unheard of in antiquity.
In the past, the Lord of Pèi also accepted Xiàng Yǔ's enfeoffment as King of Hàn,
as recorded in the ninth year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
What harm is there in that!"
He then accepted it.
The King of Wú went out to the capital's guesthouse to receive Xíng Zhēn.
When Xíng Zhēn entered the gate,
he did not dismount from his carriage.
Zhāng Zhāo said to Xíng Zhēn:
"In ritual, there is nothing not treated with respect;
in law, there is nothing not carried out.
Yet you dare to be so arrogant.
Is it because Jiāngnán is weak and small,
and lacks even an inch of blade?"
Xíng Zhēn immediately hurriedly dismounted.
The General of the Household Gentlemen, Lángyé's Xú Shèng, was indignant and angry.
Looking at his colleagues, he said:
"We, Shèng and others, cannot exert ourselves and risk our lives
to conquer Xǔ and Luò for the state,
or to annex Bā and Shǔ,
yet we allow our lord to form an alliance with Xíng Zhēn.
Is this not a disgrace!"
Tears then streamed down his face.
Xíng Zhēn heard this
and said to his followers:
"With such generals and ministers in Jiāngdōng,
they will not remain subordinate for long."
Observing Xíng Zhēn's words,
he was skilled in assessing states.
Upon his return,
did he report this to the Wèi sovereign?
However, observing that Xíng Zhēn dismounted because of Zhāng Zhāo's words,
his spirit was already broken.
The Sovereign of Wú sent the Palace Attendant, Nányáng's Zhào Zī, to present thanks.
The Emperor asked:
"What kind of sovereign
is the Sovereign of Wú?"
He replied:
"A sovereign who is intelligent, benevolent, wise, and strategically brilliant."
The Emperor asked for details.
He replied:
"Promoting Lǔ Sù from among the ordinary—this shows his intelligence;
elevating Lǚ Méng from the ranks—this shows his discernment;
capturing Yú Jìn yet not harming him—this shows his benevolence;
seizing Jīng Province without bloodshed—this shows his wisdom;
occupying three provinces and gazing fiercely upon the world—this shows his strategic brilliance;
the three provinces: Jīng, Yáng, and Jiāo.
Bowing before Your Majesty—this shows his strategic acumen."
The Emperor said:
"Does the King of Wú have much learning?"
Zhào Zī said:
"The King of Wú commands ten thousand ships upon the river,
leads a million armored troops,
appoints the worthy and employs the capable,
and his mind is set on grand strategy.
Though he has leisure time,
he extensively reads books and records,
studies historical texts,
and gathers the unusual and extraordinary,
not merely imitating scholars who search for chapters and pick out phrases."
The Emperor was fond of literary elegance,
hence Zhào Zī used these words to mock him.
"Pick out";
the Shǔ edition writes
"select."
"Can Wú be conquered?"
He replied:
"A great state has armies for conquest;
a small state has solid defenses."
These two phrases originate from Guǎnzǐ.
"Does Wú find Wèi difficult to deal with?"
He replied:
"With a million armored troops,
and the Jiāng and Hàn as its moats,
what difficulty is there!"
The Emperor said:
"How many men like you, sir, does Wú have?"
He replied:
"Those of exceptional intelligence and outstanding talent,
eighty or ninety men;
those like your servant,
could fill carts and be measured by the bushel—
they are too numerous to count."

The emperor sent an envoy to request from Wú: sparrow-head incense, large cowrie shells, bright pearls, elephant tusks, rhinoceros horns, hawksbill turtle shells, peacocks, kingfishers, fighting ducks, and long-crowing roosters.
The Běncǎo (Materia Medica) identifies xiāngfùzǐ (Cyperus rotundus) as sparrow-head incense.
This substance is found everywhere,
it is not a rarity,
so I fear it might be a different item.
Cowrie shells,
their substance is white like jade,
with purple spots forming patterns,
all arranged in orderly rows.
Bright pearls,
come from Hépǔ,
the large ones are over an inch in diameter.
Elephants come from Jiāozhǐ,
the males have two long tusks,
over ten feet long.
Rhinoceroses also come from Jiāozhǐ,
only the tōngtiānxī (pierce-the-sky rhinoceros) is most precious,
its horn has white lines like threads,
if placed among rice for chickens,
when chickens go to peck the rice,
upon seeing the horn they are startled and retreat,
southerners call it the 'startle-chicken rhinoceros'.
The hawksbill turtle's shape is like a tortoise,
its belly and back shells have burnt spots,
the large ones are like plates or bowls.
The Zhūfānzhì (Records of Various Barbarians) states: [AS-827B] The mào (hawksbill) shape is like a tortoise or soft-shelled turtle,
its back has thirteen scutes,
with black and white mottled patterns intermingled,
the edges are jagged and notched like a saw.
It has no legs but has four flippers,
the front ones long, the rear ones short,
it rows through water using its flippers to move.
The flippers and head have mottled patterns like the shell.
Older ones have thick shells with distinct black and white,
younger ones have thin shells with blurred, flowery patterns.
The common tale that the spots are formed from whipped blood
is false.
Peacocks,
are born in Luózhōu,
the males have tails of gold and emerald color,
radiant and lovely.
The Pǐyǎ (Refined Elegance) says: The Bówùzhì (Records of Broad Phenomena) states: Peacock tails change color frequently,
sometimes red, sometimes yellow,
described as like clouds and rosy clouds,
their color is not fixed.
If people clap at their tail, they dance.
The tail has gold and emerald [plumage],
which takes five years to fully form.
In the first three years of life,
the gold and emerald [plumage] is still small.
It begins to grow in early spring,
and after three or four months it sheds again,
flourishing and withering along with the flower calyxes.
People collect their tails to adorn fans and dusters,
if taken from a live bird, the gold and emerald color does not fade.
Southerners who take their tails,
grasp a knife, hiding in dense bamboo in concealed places,
wait for it to pass,
then swiftly cut its tail,
if not severed immediately,
it turns its head to look back once,
and the gold and emerald [plumage] loses its luster.
Whenever it wishes to rest briefly,
it first chooses a place to position its tail.
Therefore, to capture one alive,
wait for heavy rain then go to seize it,
its tail gets wet and heavy,
unable to soar high,
even if people approach,
it still loves its tail,
and will not fly away.
Kingfishers,
are about the size of sparrows,
the male red ones are called fěi,
the female blue-green ones are called cuì,
their feathers can be used for adornment.
Ducks are tame and familiar,
but ones capable of fighting are hard to find.
As for long-crowing roosters,
their crowing sound is long.
"Jīng and Yáng provinces,
have regular statutes for tribute.
Yǔ demarcated the nine provinces,
assigning tribute according to the land's produce,
this is the regular statute.
This [request] is not according to ritual,
it should not be granted."
The King of Wú said:
"We are currently engaged in matters in the northwest,
meaning contending with Shǔ,
and also must prepare against Wèi.
We rely on our lord for our mandate.
What he requests,
is to us like tiles and stones,
why should I begrudge it!
Moreover, he is in the period of liáng'ān [mourning seclusion]
yet makes requests like these,
how can one discuss ritual with him!"
He supplied them all.
The historian states the emperor was spied upon by the enemy state.
22 The King of Wú appointed his son Sūn Dēng as heir apparent,
and excellently selected teachers and friends: with Zhūgě Jǐn's son Zhūgě Kè, the Administrator of Nánjùn, and Zhāng Zhāo's son Zhāng Xiū, the Suīyuǎn General,
according to Shěn Yuē's records,
there were forty numbered generals,
Suīyuǎn being the fourteenth.
They entered [the palace] to lecture on the Shī and Shū,
and went out to accompany [him] in riding and archery,
they were called the 'Four Friends'.
Dēng received his officials and subordinates,
roughly using the etiquette for commoners.
23 In the twelfth month,
the emperor traveled on an eastern inspection tour.
24 The emperor wished to enfeoff the King of Wú's son Dēng as a marquis of ten thousand households,
the King of Wú, considering Dēng young,
submitted a letter declining and not accepting;
he again sent Wúxīng native
Shěn Héng, the Western Section Official, to enter and give thanks,
the Xìngpǔ (Genealogy of Surnames) states: The Shěn surname comes from Wúxīng,
originally from Dān Jì, the tenth son of King Wén of Zhōu,
who was enfeoffed with the revenue from Shěn,
which is the Shěn Pavilion in Píngyú, Rǔnán,
his descendants took the state as their surname.
And also from Prince Zhēn, son of King Zhuāng of Chǔ, enfeoffed at Shěnlù,
his descendants included Shěn Yǐnshù, Shěn Zhūliáng.
Héng,
is pronounced xíng.
The emperor asked:
"Does Wú suspect Wèi will move eastward?"
Héng said:
"We do not suspect."
Said:
"Why?"
Said:
"We trust and rely on the old alliance,
speaking of returning to good relations,
therefore we do not suspect;
if Wèi violates the alliance,
we naturally have preparations."
He asked further:
"I have heard the heir apparent is to come,
is this true?"
Héng said:
"Your servant is in the eastern court,
does not sit in court,
does not participate in banquets,
Wú is east of the river,
hence called the eastern court.
'Does not sit in court, does not participate in banquets',
records the words of Yǐn Shāngyáng in the Tángōng chapter of the Lǐjì.
Court,
is pronounced zhāo.
I have heard nothing."
The emperor approved of him.
The King of Wú at Wǔchāng by the fishing terrace
the Shuǐjīng (Water Classic) states,
Wǔchāng has Fán Mountain,
north facing the great river,
on the river is a fishing terrace.
became greatly drunk,
and had people splash water on the ministers
who were drunk,
splashing water on them to wake them,
so they could then drink.
"Today we drink to the full,
only when drunk we fall from the terrace,
then shall we stop!"
Zhāng Zhāo looked stern and said nothing,
went outside,
and sat in his carriage.
The king sent someone to call Zhāo back in,
and said to him:

The Palace Attendant Lú Yù said:

The sage kings of old only feared not hearing of their faults.
This is why we ministers are not as good as Lóng."
The Emperor then relented.
Yù
was the son of Zhí.
8. In the twelfth month,
on the guǐsì day,
Yǐngyīn Jìng Hóu Chén Qún died.
The rules for posthumous titles: Respectful of self and sparing of words is called jìng;
broad-minded, joyful, and ending well is called jìng.
Whenever he submitted sealed memorials,
he would destroy the drafts,
so that people of the time and even his own children could not know their contents.
Some critics ridiculed Qún for holding office in a posture of clasped hands and silence;
meaning he merely clasped his hands,
silent without a word.
An edict ordered the compilation of Qún's submitted memorials to be used as the Memorials of Famous Ministers,
and only then did the court officials see Qún's remonstrances,
and all sighed in admiration.
Yuán Zǐ's Discussion says: Some say:
"Is not the Shaofǔ Yáng Fù a loyal minister?
When he saw his ruler's faults, he would vehemently confront them,
and in conversation with others, he never failed to speak of them."
Speaking of them,
means to talk about them.
"The benevolent love others;
applying this to the ruler is called loyalty,
applying it to parents is called filial piety.
Now, as a minister,
seeing his ruler lose the Way,
strenuously criticizing his faults and broadcasting his misdeeds,
may be called a forthright gentleman,
but is not a loyal minister.
Therefore, the late Minister of Works Chén Qún was not like this;
he would converse all day,
yet never spoke of his ruler's faults;
he submitted several tens of memorials,
but outsiders did not know.
The gentleman says that Qún was thus a man of noble character."
9. On the yǐwèi day,
the Emperor traveled to Xǔchāng.
8. Gōngsūn Yuān repeatedly spoke ill words in front of guests from within the state.
The Emperor wished to campaign against him,
and appointed Wúqiū Jiǎn, the Inspector of Jīng Province,
as the Inspector of Yōu Province.
Wúqiū,
is a compound surname.
Wú,
is pronounced like "wú."
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
there has been nothing worthy of record.
Wú and Shǔ rely on their perilous terrain,
and cannot be quickly pacified.
We might as well use the idle troops from this region to conquer Liáodōng."
Zhèng Xuán said: Liáo,
is a word meaning 'tentatively' or 'roughly.'
"All that Jiǎn has proposed are minor tactics from the Warring States period,
not matters befitting a true king.
Wú raises troops year after year,
chēng,
means to raise.
Yet we still keep our armor stored and nurture our soldiers,
and have not decisively launched a campaign against them,
truly because the common people are weary and exhausted.
Yuān was born and raised beyond the seas,
having inherited [rule] for three generations,
[Gōngsūn] Dù, [Gōngsūn] Kāng, [Gōngsūn] Yuān,
altogether three generations.
Zhǎng,
is pronounced zhǎng.
Internally, he cultivates warfare and archery,
yet Jiǎn wishes to drive deep with a flank army,
arriving in the morning and rolling up [the enemy] by evening—
we know this is reckless."
The Emperor did not listen,
and sent Jiǎn to command the various armies along with the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán, stationing them on the southern border of Liáodōng,
and summoning Yuān by an imperial edict.
Yuān then raised troops in rebellion,
and met Jiǎn in battle at Liáosuì.
Liáosuì County,
belonged to Liáodōng Commandery during the two Hàn dynasties;
the Jìn records do not mention this place,
likely it was on the eastern bank of the Liáo River.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: In Gāogōulí County of Xuāntú Commandery, there is Liáo Mountain,
from which the Lesser Liáo River flows,
running southwest to Liáosuì County,
and entering the Greater Liáo River.
Xǐ,
is pronounced sǐ.
The Liáo River rose greatly in flood,
and Jiǎn, engaging in battle, fared poorly,
leading his army back to Yòuběipíng.
Yuān consequently proclaimed himself King of Yān,
changed his reign era to Shàohàn,
established all the officials,
sent envoys to bestow the seal of the Xiānbēi Chányú,
enfeoffed and appointed the border people,
and incited the Xiānbēi to invade and harass the northern regions.
9. The Hàn Empress Zhāng passed away.
10. In the ninth month,
great floods occurred in Jì, Yǎn, Xú, and Yù provinces.
Jì Province governed Zhào, Jùlù, Ānpíng, Píngyuán, Lèlíng, Bóhǎi, Héjiān, Bólíng, Qīnghé, Zhōngshān, and Chángshān.
Xú Province governed Péngchéng, Xiàpī, Dōnghǎi, Lángyá, Guǎnglíng, and Línhuái.
Yù Province governed Yǐngchuān, Rǔnán, Rǔyīn, Liáng, Pèi, Qiáo, Lǔ, Yìyáng, and Ānfēng.
11. Lady Guō of Xīpíng enjoyed the Emperor's favor.
The lady was from a great clan of Héyòu,
during the Huángchū era,
because her commandery rebelled,
she was confiscated and entered the palace.
The Emperor was touring the rear garden,
holding a private banquet with extreme pleasure.
Qūyàn,
means a banquet within the palace grounds,
akin to saying a private banquet.
Lè,
is pronounced luò;
the same below.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and consequently forbade his attendants from making it public.
Xuān,
means to announce,
to reveal the matter.
The next day,
she said to the Emperor:
"Yesterday, you toured and feasted in the northern garden,
was it pleasant?"
The rear garden was at the northern corner of Luò City.
Over ten people were killed.
On the Gēngchén day,
the Empress was ordered to commit suicide,
yet she was still posthumously honored with the title Dào.
The rules for posthumous titles state: Dying young in middle age is called Dào;
acting recklessly without propriety is called Dào.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
she was buried at Mǐnlíng.
Her younger brother, [Máo] Zēng, was transferred to be a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
12. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Emperor adopted Gāotáng Lóng's proposal,
and constructed the Yuánqiū altar at Wěisù Mountain south of Luòyáng.
The Wèishì Chūnqiū states: Luòyáng has Wěisù Mountain,
located in Yīnxiāng,
which the Wèi period developed into the Yuánqiū altar.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Wěisù Mountain is twenty lǐ south of Luòyáng.
"In the early days of the Hàn dynasty,
inheriting the aftermath of the Qín's destruction of learning,
they gathered and collected the fragmented and incomplete [texts],
to prepare for the suburban sacrifices.
For over four hundred years,
the Dì sacrifice was abandoned and not performed.
The Cáo clan's lineage descends from Yǒuyú,
so now we sacrifice to the August Sovereign Emperor of Heaven at the Yuánqiū altar,
matching him with the founding ancestor, Emperor Shùn of Yú;
sacrifice to the August Sovereign Empress of Earth at the Fāngqiū altar,
matching her with Shùn's clan, the Yīshì;
Shùn,
was Yáo's son-in-law.
Yáo,
was of the Yīqí clan.
matching him with Emperor Wǔ;
sacrifice to the Earthly Deity at the northern suburb,
matching her with Empress Wǔxuān."
13. Lǚ Xí, the Registrar of Lújiāng, secretly sent someone to request troops from Wú,
wishing to open the city gates and act as an insider.
The Lord of Wú sent General of the Guards Quán Cóng to supervise Former General Zhū Huán and others to go to his aid.
Once they arrived,
the affair was exposed,
and the Wú army returned.
14. Zhūgé Kè arrived at Dānyáng,
and circulated documents to the senior officials of the four subordinate commanderies/cities,
"Sìbù",
should be
"sìjùn",
meaning Wú, Kuàijī, Xīndū, and Póyáng commanderies,
all adjacent to Dānyáng,
where the Shānyuè relied on the rugged terrain to appear and disappear,
hence he ordered each to guard its own borders.
Some say: Sìbù,
refers to the four Commandants of the Eastern, Western, Southern, and Northern Divisions.
He clearly established military units;
those common people who submitted to transformation,
he ordered all to settle in garrisoned communities.
Then he sent the various generals inward,
deploying troops in secluded and obstructed areas,
making the various generals enter and hold the secluded and obstructed lands,
hence it is called 'nèi' (to send in).
Nèi,
is read as nà.
He did not engage them in battle,
but waited until their grain crops were about to ripen,
then repeatedly sent troops to reap and cut them down,
leaving no seed behind.
Once the old grain was exhausted,
and the new grain could not be harvested,
and the common people were settled in garrisoned communities,
they had virtually nothing to obtain.
Thereupon, the mountain people grew hungry and destitute,
and gradually came out to surrender.
Kè then again issued an order stating:
"When mountain people abandon evil and submit to transformation,
they should all be comforted and consoled,
and moved out to outer counties.
Do not be suspicious or doubtful,
and do not detain or arrest them!"
Hú Kàng, the Chief of Jiǔyáng, captured the surrendered commoner Zhōu Yí;
since Jiǔyáng had a Chief appointed,
it must have been made a county,
its location should be within Dānyáng Commandery,
but now it cannot be verified.
Kàng bound him and sent him to the commandery office.
Kè, considering Kàng had violated the order,
then beheaded him as a warning.
When the people heard that Kàng was executed for arresting a person,
they understood that the officials only wished for them to come out,
and thereupon the old and young supported each other and came out.
The annual quota of people,
was all as originally planned;
the annual quota of people is seen in the second year of Qīnglóng in the previous scroll.
The remainder was distributed among the various generals.
The Lord of Wú praised his achievements,
and appointed Kè as General Who Inspires Awe in the North,
General Who Inspires Awe in the North,
was also a position created by the Sūn clan.
He transferred [Kè] to station troops at Wǎnkǒu in Lújiāng.
The Wǎn River flows southeast from Huòshān County for three hundred and forty lǐ into the Great River,
which is called Wǎnkǒu.
Wǎn,
is pronounced huǎn.
In this year,
the bell stands, camels, bronze statues, and dew-collecting basins from Cháng'ān were moved to Luòyáng.
The basins broke during transport,
and the sound was heard for dozens of lǐ.
The bronze statues were too heavy
to transport,
so they were left at Bàchéng.
Bàchéng
was the old city of Bàlíng County, Jīngzhào Commandery of the Hàn dynasty.
They were called Wēngzhòng,
and were placed seated outside the Simǎ Gate.
Additionally, one yellow dragon and one fenghuang were cast;
the dragon was four zhàng tall,
and the fenghuang was over three zhàng tall.
They were placed in front of the inner palace hall.
An earthen hill was constructed at the northwestern corner of the Fānglín Garden.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Inside the Dàxià Gate, on the eastern side near the wall, there is Jǐngyáng Mountain,
which is the northwestern corner of the Fānglín Garden.
Péi Sōngzhī said: Fānglín Garden is the present Huálín Garden.
When Prince Fáng of Qí ascended the throne,
it was renamed Huálín Garden.
陬 (zōu),
pronounced as jiāng hóu fān.
Pines, bamboos, various trees, and fine grasses were planted on it,
and mountain birds and various wild animals were captured and placed within.
The Army Discussion Clerk of the Minister over the Masses, Dǒng Xún, submitted a memorial remonstrating:
The Hàn dynasty's ducal offices did not have an Army Discussion Clerk;
this official position was established by Wèi.
掾 (yuàn),
pronounced as yú juàn fān.
"Your servant has heard that in ancient times, upright men
spoke their utmost for the state,
without fearing death.
Thus, Zhōu Chāng compared Gāozǔ to Jié and Zhòu,
and Liú Fǔ likened Empress Zhào to a servant girl.
Zhōu Chāng
has been annotated previously.
Liú Fǔ's affair is seen in the thirty-first scroll, in the first year of the Yǒngshǐ era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
Even if faced with naked blades and boiling water,
they would advance without looking back,
truly because they cherished the realm for the ruler of their time.
Since the Jiàn'ān era,
deaths in field battles,
or households completely wiped out,
even if some survivors remain,
they are orphaned, elderly, or weak.
If the current palace buildings are narrow and small,
and they should be expanded,
it should still be done according to the season,
without hindering agricultural work.
How much more so for creating useless objects?
The yellow dragon, fenghuang,
nine dragons, and dew-collecting basins—
these are all things that sage and enlightened rulers do not promote.
Their labor cost is three times that of palace halls.
Your Majesty has already honored your ministers,
distinguishing them with caps and coronets,
clothing them in embroidered silks,
and carrying them in ornate carriages,
to set them apart from petty men.
Yet now you make them dig squares and lift earth—
方 (fāng),
means digging earth to form squares.
The so-called 'fāng zhōng' in the Hànshū
also carries this meaning.
Their caps and garments in tatters,
了鸟 (liǎo niǎo),
describes the appearance of caps and garments being worn and torn.
This is highly inappropriate.
Confucius said:
'The ruler employs his ministers according to ritual;
the ministers serve their ruler with loyalty.'
See the Analects, Confucius's words to Duke Dìng of Lǔ.
How can the state be established otherwise!
Your servant knows that speaking out will certainly lead to death,
but your servant compares himself to a single hair on an ox.
Alive, I am of no benefit;
dead, what loss is there?
Sīmǎ Qiān, in his letter replying to Rèn Ān, said: If I were to submit to the law and be executed,
it would be like losing one hair from nine oxen—
what difference would it make from an ant?
My heart bids farewell to the world.
Your servant has eight sons.
After your servant's death,
they will be a burden to Your Majesty!"
When about to submit the memorial,
he bathed and awaited orders.
The Emperor said:
"Is Dǒng Xún not afraid of death?"
The officials in charge requested to arrest Xún,
but an edict was issued not to interrogate him.
Gāotáng Lóng submitted a memorial stating:
"The petty men of this age
delight in discussing the extravagance and waste of Qín and Hàn to corrupt Your Sacred Majesty's mind;
they seek to obtain the immoderate vessels of perished states—
'immoderate vessels'
refers to the bell stands, camels, bronze statues, and dew-collecting basins from Cháng'ān—
to preserve the blessings of the divine and enlightened."
The Emperor did not listen.
Lóng again submitted a memorial:
"In ancient times, the floodwaters reached the heavens for twenty-two years.
Lóng's statement here
likely takes from Gǔn's nine years of toil without success,
and Yǔ's thirteen years regulating Yǎnzhōu,
combining them to make the number twenty-two years.
载 (zǎi),
pronounced as zǐ hài fān.
Now there is no urgency like that time,
yet you make the dukes, ministers, and senior officials labor together with servants and laborers on construction projects.
When the Four Barbarians hear of this,
it is not a good reputation;
when recorded in bamboo and silk,
it is not a fine name.
Now the two bandits, Wú and Shǔ,
are not merely tribes from barren lands, minor barbarians, or bandits gathering in villages—
'barren lands'
refers to the great deserts where no grass or trees grow,
with much white sand.
'Minor barbarians'
refers to the Wūhuán
and Xiānbēi.
'Bandits gathering in villages'
refers to thieves and bandits who arise secretly,
occupying villages and settlements.
They wish to contend for supremacy with the Central Kingdom.
衡 (héng)
is used to weigh lightness and heaviness.
'Contending for supremacy' means
that Wú and Shǔ themselves consider their state's power equal to the Central Kingdom's,
with neither side being lighter or heavier.
'If Quán and Shàn both cultivate virtuous governance,
reduce and lighten taxes and levies,
frequently consult the aged and worthy,
and conduct affairs in accordance with ritual and measure,'
if Your Majesty hears this,
would you not feel apprehensive and dislike them for being so,
considering them difficult to quickly subdue and exterminate,
and thus worry for the state?
But if the informant says: 'Those two bandits both act without the Way,
promoting extravagance without measure,
conscripting their officers and people,
increasing their taxes and levies,
so that those below cannot bear the burden,
and lamentations grow daily more severe,'
if Your Majesty hears this,
would you not then be glad of their exhaustion and find it not difficult to seize them?
If it is so,
then one can change perspective and consider,
and the principle of affairs is not far off!
The rulers of perished states themselves believed they would not perish,
and then proceeded to perish.
The sage and worthy rulers themselves believed they might perish,
and then proceeded not to perish.
Now the realm is impoverished and depleted,
the people have not even a dàn or shí of stored grain,
the state has no provisions to last the year,
externally there are powerful enemies,
the six armies are exposed on the borders,
internally construction works are undertaken,
the commanderies and prefectures are in turmoil.
If bandit alarms arise,
then your servant fears the soldiers working on the earthen walls will not be able to throw themselves against the enemy's court.
Moreover,
the salaries of generals and officials
have gradually been reduced;
compared to the past,
they are now one-fifth.
Those who receive retirement benefits have also had their stipends and grants cut off;
those who should not have to pay now all contribute half.
This means the government's income is much more than before,
while its expenditures are about one-third less than in the past.
参 (cān)
means one-third.
Yet repeatedly there is insufficiency,
and small levies on beef
follow one after another.
This is likely to reward and feast the laborers and artisans,
as the funds allocated for expenses are insufficient to supply them,
hence the beef levy to provide for it.
度 (duó),
pronounced as tuó luò fān.
All these various expenses
must have a destination.
This points out that the various expenses are all in construction and repair.
These are what the ruler uses to kindly nurture the officials and people and act as their master of fate.
If they are now abolished,
it is to take away their fate.
Having obtained them and then losing them—
this is the source of resentment."
The Emperor read it
and said to the Directors and Chiefs of the Central Secretariat:
"Reading Lóng's memorial
makes me fearful!"
The Directors and Chiefs of the Central Secretariat
were in charge of memorial affairs;
because the Emperor read Lóng's memorial, he thus spoke to them.
The Minister of Works, Wèi Jì, submitted a memorial stating:
"Now, many of those who discuss affairs are fond of pleasing the ear:
when they speak of governance,
they compare Your Majesty to Yáo and Shùn;
when they speak of military campaigns,
they compare the two enemies to foxes and rats.
I believe this is not so.
Within the Four Seas,
the land is divided into three parts,
with men of talent exerting their strength,
each serving their own lord.
This is no different from the division of governance among the Six States.
At present, for a thousand *lǐ* there is no smoke from hearths,
the remnant people suffer hardship and distress;
if Your Majesty does not pay careful attention to this,
the situation will decline into ruin,
and it will be difficult to revive it again.
In the time of Emperor Wǔ,
the food in the rear palace did not exceed one meat dish,
clothing did not use brocade or embroidery,
mats and cushions were not adorned with borders,
and utensils were not painted with cinnabar lacquer.
In ancient times, simplicity and plainness were valued.
When Shùn created lacquered vessels, his ministers remonstrated without cease;
how much more so with the addition of cinnabar!
He left blessings for his descendants,
all of which Your Majesty has observed.
The urgent tasks of the present day
should involve both ruler and ministers, high and low,
calculating the resources of the treasury,
measuring income to determine expenditure,
yet even then we fear it will not be enough;
but now, labor conscription does not cease,
extravagance and waste grow daily more esteemed,
and the storehouses are daily depleted.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn believed in the ways of immortals,
saying he should obtain dew from above the clouds to consume with powdered jade,
and thus erected immortal-hand vessels to catch the high dew.
Your Majesty, being enlightened,
often criticized and laughed at this.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sought dew and was still criticized;
Your Majesty has no need for dew yet emptily sets up such vessels,
which adds nothing to what is good but wastes effort and resources.
Truly, these are matters that should be curtailed by Your Majesty's sagely consideration!"
At that time, there was an edict to seize the wives
(seize means to take)
of soldiers
and return them to be matched with soldiers,
allowing them to redeem themselves with captives,
and also selecting those among them with beauty to be taken into the rear palace.
(Beauty refers to those with attractive appearance;
head refers to those with thick, black hair.)
"Your Majesty
is the Son of Heaven,
and the common people, officials, and subjects
are also Your Majesty's children.
Now, to take from those and give to these
is no different from taking an elder brother's wife and giving her to a younger brother as a wife.
This shows partiality in the parental kindness.
Furthermore,
the edict allows one to substitute with a captive of comparable age and appearance to one's wife,
so the wealthy exhaust their family fortunes and property,
while the poor borrow and incur debt,
buying captives at high prices to redeem their wives.
The county authorities use matching with soldiers as a pretext but in reality take them into the rear palace,
and the ugly ones are then given out to the soldiers.
Those who obtain wives are not necessarily pleased, while those who lose their wives are certainly sorrowful,
some impoverished, some distressed,
all discontented.
A ruler who possesses the world but fails to win the hearts of the myriad people
rarely avoids peril.
Moreover, the armies outside number several hundred thousand men,
and the daily expenses are not merely a thousand pieces of gold.
Even if we devote the entire empire's taxes to support this campaign,
it will still be insufficient,
let alone that there are also women in the rear palace who are beyond the established number and unregistered.
(Beyond the number refers to those outside the official quota.
Unregistered means those whose names are not on the palace register.)
(Fù is pronounced fú yòu fān.)
Rewards and gifts are lavishly bestowed,
with internal and external demands,
their expenses amounting to half the military expenditure.
(This means the expenses are half of what is spent on the army.)
Mounding earth to form mountains,
digging the ground to make seas,
(refers to opening the Kūnmíng Pond;
mounding earth to form mountains
refers to constructing the Three Divine Mountains and the Jiàntái.)
and none dare to oppose it.
Since the decline and chaos began,
for forty or fifty years,
horses have not left their saddles,
soldiers have not removed their armor,
with powerful enemies at the borders,
plotting to endanger the Wèi house.
Your Majesty does not act with caution and diligence,
mindful of promoting frugality,
but instead pursues extravagance and waste.
The Central Imperial Workshop produces playthings and curiosities.
(The *Jìn Shū* records: The Shàofǔ oversees the Central, Left, and Right Imperial Workshops.)
These indeed please the eyes and ears,
but they are also enough to encourage the hearts of our enemies!
Alas,
to abandon the frugality of Yáo and Shùn and instead engage in the extravagant affairs of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn—
I privately believe this is not something Your Majesty should adopt."
The Emperor did not heed him.
Gāotáng Lóng was critically ill,
and dictated a memorial, saying:
(Being critically ill and unable to write himself,
he dictated and had someone else write it down.)
"Zēngzǐ once said: 'When a man is about to die,
his words are good.'
(See the *Analects*.)
I have often feared sudden death,
with my loyal sincerity not made clear.
My sincere devotion
hopes that Your Majesty will deign to reflect upon it!
I observe that when the Three Dynasties possessed the world,
sage and worthy rulers succeeded one another,
lasting for several hundred years.
Not an inch of land was not theirs,
not a single person was not their subject.
Yet men like Jié and Zhòu
indulged their hearts and exhausted their desires,
causing August Heaven to be enraged,
and their ancestral states to become ruins.
Zhòu's head was displayed on a white banner.
(King Wǔ cut off Zhòu's head
and hung it on the Tàibái banner.
Xiāo is pronounced jiān yáo fān.)
Shāng Tāng defeated Jié at Míngtiáo,
and then exiled him to Náncháo.
(Kǒng Ānguó said: Míngtiáo was located west of Ānyì.)
Tāng and Wǔ possessed the world;
were they different men?
They were all descendants of enlightened kings.
During the Huángchū era,
Heaven gave warning signs,
with birds of a different kind
being raised in swallows' nests,
their beaks, claws, and breasts red.
This was a great portent for the Wèi house.
(The *Jìn Shū* Treatise on the Five Elements records: In the first year of Huángchū,
in the Wèiyāng Palace, a swallow gave birth to a hawk,
with beak and claws both red.
Zhǎng is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.)
Regarding the affairs of the Sīmǎ clan,
Lóng certainly foresaw them.
Those who command the state and oversee the military
are often positioned like chess pieces,
guarding and pacifying the imperial domain,
assisting and illuminating the imperial house.
Now, August Heaven shows no partiality;
it aids only the virtuous.
(Words from the 'Cài Zhòng zhī Mìng' chapter of the *Shū*.)
If there is virtue above, then the mandate is extended beyond its allotted span;
if there is resentment and lamentation below,
then the record is withdrawn and given to the capable.
(Lù refers to the chart records.)
The world is the world of all under Heaven,
not solely Your Majesty's world!"
The Emperor issued a handwritten edict deeply consoling and commending him.
Not long after, he died.
Chén Shòu commented: Gāotáng Lóng's learning was cultivated and brilliant,
his will set on rectifying his ruler.
He presented admonitions based on changing circumstances,
arising from sincere earnestness—
how loyal he was!
But when it came to insisting on changing the calendar,
making Wèi follow Yú,
this was what is called 'the idea exceeding the understanding'!
(Referring to the discussion that year about the appearance of the yellow dragon.)
'The idea exceeding the understanding'
means that his conjectural theory
was held too firmly,
exceeding what his learning had thoroughly mastered.
The Emperor deeply detested those who were ostentatious and superficial.
He issued an edict to the Minister of Personnel, Lù Yù, saying:
"In selecting and recommending officials, do not choose those who merely have a reputation.
A reputation is like drawing a cake on the ground—
it cannot be eaten."
Lù Yù replied:
"Reputation may not be sufficient to attract extraordinary talents, but it can obtain ordinary officials.
Ordinary officials fear instruction and admire goodness,
and only then do they gain a reputation.
This is not something to be detested.
I, your foolish minister, am not capable of recognizing extraordinary talents,
and those in charge are precisely tasked with following reputations and adhering to conventions.
However, there should be means to verify their subsequent performance.
In ancient times, officials presented their proposals through words,
