10 The Lord of Wú ordered the Secretariat Gentleman Lǚ Yī to oversee the auditing of documents from various government offices and commanderies,
Yī gradually abused his power,
using harsh laws and clever slander,
framing the innocent,
defaming and undermining high officials,
reporting even the slightest faults.
Crown Prince Dēng repeatedly remonstrated,
the Lord of Wú did not listen,
court officials dared not speak further,
all feared him and averted their eyes.
First, Wū Bái falsely accused the former Jiāngxià Prefect Diāo Jiā of slandering state affairs.
The Lord of Wú was enraged,
arrested Jiā,
and imprisoned him for interrogation.
At the time, all those implicated feared Wū,
who was among those implicated with Jiā.
Implicated,
(pronounced) cú wò fān.
Only Shì Yí, the Palace Attendant from Běihǎi, said he had not heard anything.
Shì,
a surname;
Yí,
a given name.
Yí originally had the surname Shì.
Kǒng Róng mocked Yí, saying the character "shì" (氏) looked like "mín" (民) without a head on top,
so he changed his surname to Shì (是).
After several days,
the imperial decree grew increasingly severe,
and the officials held their breath in fear.
Yí said:
"Now the blade and saw are already at my neck.
How would I dare to conceal anything for Jiā,
bringing destruction upon myself,
and becoming a disloyal ghost!
I only say what I have heard and know, which should have a beginning and an end."
He answered the questions based on the facts,
and his words did not waver.
The Lord of Wú then released him;
Jiā was also spared.
The Grand General Lù Xùn and the Minister of Ceremonies Pān Jùn were worried that Wū would bring chaos to the state.
Whenever they spoke of it,
they would shed tears.
Wū reported the faults of Chancellor Gù Yōng,
and the Lord of Wú was angry,
reprimanding Yōng.
The Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate Xiè Hóng asked Wū during a conversation:
"How is Lord Gù's situation?"
Wū said:
"Not good."
Hóng asked again:
"If this lord is dismissed,
who should replace him?"
Wū did not answer.
Hóng said:
"Could it be that Minister of Ceremonies Pān will get it?"
Wū
said:
"What you say is close."
Hóng said:
"Minister of Ceremonies Pān often gnashes his teeth at you,
but he has no way to act.
He wants to report and accuse you of crimes, but it is not within the duties of the Minister of Ceremonies,
so he has no way to do it.
I fear he will attack you tomorrow!"
Under the Hàn system,
the Chancellor and the Imperial Counselor reported and accused officials who had committed crimes.
Thus, Yōng's matter was dropped.
Pān Jùn requested to come to court,
and went to Jiànyè.
Jùn originally stayed in Wǔchāng.
Come to court,
(pronounced) zhí yáo fān.
When he arrived,
he heard that Crown Prince Sūn Dēng had already spoken of it many times.
Upon arriving in Jiànyè, he learned that the Crown Prince had spoken of Wū's matters many times.
Jùn then invited all the officials to a grand banquet,
intending to kill Wū with his own hands during the gathering,
taking the responsibility upon himself,
taking upon himself the crime of killing with his own hands.
Wū secretly learned of this,
and claimed illness, not attending.
The Commander of Xīlíng, Bù Zhì, submitted a memorial saying:
"Gù Yōng, Lù Xùn, and Pān Jùn
are dedicated to serving with utmost sincerity,
unable to rest or eat in peace,
thinking of how to bring stability to the state and benefit the people,
and establishing long-term plans.
They can be called loyal ministers who are the heart, backbone, and limbs of the state.
They should each be entrusted with their duties,
and no other officials should supervise their work,
or evaluate their performance.
If these three ministers fail to consider something, that is one thing,
but how would they dare to deceive their sovereign!"
The sovereign,
is like heaven.
The Left General Zhū Jù's troops were supposed to receive thirty thousand strings of cash,
but the artisan Wáng Suì fraudulently took them.
Wū suspected that Jù had actually taken them,
and interrogated the responsible officer.
The responsible officer,
was Jù's military officer.
Jù pitied his innocence,
and gave him a lavish burial.
Wū then reported that Jù's officer had concealed things for Jù,
hence the lavish funeral.
The Lord of Wú repeatedly questioned and reprimanded Jù,
and Jù had no way to prove his innocence,
lying on straw awaiting punishment.
After several days,
the Army Supervisor Liú Zhù discovered,
and said that Wáng Suì had taken it.
Liú Zhù discovered the matter and spoke of it.
He said:
"If even Zhū Jù is wronged,
how much more so the officials and common people!"
Then they thoroughly investigated Wū's crimes,
and rewarded Zhù with a million cash.
Chancellor Yōng went to the Court of Judicial Review to adjudicate the case,
and Wū appeared as a prisoner.
Yōng, with a gentle expression, asked him about the details of the case.
As he was about to leave,
he said to Wū:
"Do you perhaps wish to say something?"
Say,
means to speak.
At the time, the Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat Huái Xù
Huái,
a surname;
Xù,
a given name.
According to the Genealogy of Surnames: descendants of the Wúhuái clan.
Yōng reprimanded Xù, saying:
"The state has proper laws,
how could it come to this!"
The responsible officials recommended that Wū be executed by decapitation,
and some thought he should be burned and torn apart,
to make an example of the arch-villain.
King Zhòu of Shāng used the punishment of roasting on a bronze pillar,
Xiàng Yǔ burned Jì Xìn to death,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn burned Sū Wén on the Héng Bridge,
but these were not established as formal punishments.
Wáng Mǎng instituted the punishment of burning,
but later generations did not follow it.
Tearing apart,
refers to tearing apart by chariots,
the ancient punishment of dismemberment.
Zé said:
"In a prosperous and enlightened age,
such punishments should not be revived."
The Lord of Wú followed this advice.
After Lǚ Yī was executed,
the ruler of Wú sent the Secretariat Gentleman Yuán Lǐ to convey apologies to the various senior generals,
and to inquire about what policies should be abolished or implemented at the time.
When Yuán Lǐ returned,
an edict was issued reprimanding Zhūgě Jǐn, Bù Zhì, Zhū Rán, Lǚ Dài, and others, stating:
"Yuán Lǐ reported upon his return: 'When I met with Zǐyú, Zǐshān, Yìfēng, and Dìnggōng,
Zhūgě Jǐn,
styled Zǐyú.
Bù Zhì,
styled Zǐshān.
Zhū Rán,
styled Yìfēng.
Lǚ Dài,
styled Dìnggōng.
Jǐn,
pronounced qú lìn fān.
Zhì,
pronounced zhí rì fān.
I asked which matters should be prioritized and which should be deferred.
They were unwilling to provide a full account,
and instead deferred to Bówén and Chéngmíng.
Bówén and Chéngmíng, upon meeting me, wept with sincere distress,
their words filled with hardship,
even to the point of harboring fear and apprehension,
showing signs of unease.'
Hearing this, I was deeply troubled and
profoundly perplexed!
Perplexed,
meaning puzzled.
Only sages can be free from faults in their actions,
and the wise can perceive their own errors.
How can all of a person's actions
be entirely correct?
If I alone have caused offense by rejecting the opinions of the multitude,
yet remain unaware of it,
then it is natural for you, gentlemen, to harbor doubts and difficulties.
If not for this,
how could things have come to this point?
In working with you, gentlemen,
from youth to old age,
my hair has turned two colors—
two colors,
meaning streaked with gray.
Shǎo,
pronounced shì zhào fān.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
In both public and private matters, our interests are sufficiently aligned to protect one another.
Though our relationship is that of ruler and subject in principle,
in affection, it is akin to that of flesh and blood.
We share in honor, fortune, joy, and sorrow.
Loyalty does not conceal true feelings,
and wisdom does not withhold strategies.
Matters are judged by right and wrong;
if words and actions are right,
then ruler and subject share in the right;
if wrong,
then they share in the wrong.
We are like passengers on the same boat crossing a river—
who among us would change this?
Yì,
pronounced as the character.
Guǎn Zhòng never failed to remonstrate,
and Duke Huán never failed to heed advice.
Even when his advice was not accepted,
he persisted in remonstrating without cease.
Now, upon reflection, I lack the virtue of Duke Huán,
yet you, gentlemen, have not even voiced your remonstrances,
still clinging to doubts and difficulties.
In light of this,
I am indeed superior to Duke Huán of Qí,
but I wonder how you, gentlemen, compare to Guǎn Zhòng!"
Subordinates follow their superiors not by obeying orders but by aligning with their intentions.
Sūn Quán claimed to be superior to Duke Huán of Qí,
yet demanded that his ministers emulate Guǎn Zhòng.
Even if Wú truly had a Guǎn Zhòng,
he would not dare speak fully to Sūn Quán,
as can be seen from the case of Lù Xùn.
In winter, the eleventh month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Sīkōng Wèi Zhēn was appointed as Sītú,
and the Colonel-Director of Retainers Cuī Lín was appointed as Sīkōng.
In the twelfth month,
Jiǎng Wǎn of Shǔ advanced and stationed troops in Hànzhōng.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor fell ill.
On the Xīnsì day,
Lady Guō was established as Empress.
15. Initially,
when Tàizǔ was the Duke of Wèi,
he established the position of Zànlìng, appointing Liú Fàng
(from Zàn County,
which during the Hàn Dynasty belonged to Pèi Commandery;
Wáng Mǎng changed its name to Zànzhì;
during Wèi, it was divided and placed under Qiáo Commandery).
Some say that "zàn"
means "to assist."
In general, when issuing orders, one is made to assist and support,
hence it was adopted as an official title.
This was likely established within Wèi Wǔ's hegemonial administration.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he renamed the Secretariat as the Central Secretariat,
appointing Fàng as its Supervisor
and Zī as its Director,
thereby placing them in charge of confidential matters.
In the second year of the Yánxī era of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
the position of Secretariat Supervisor was established;
when Wèi Wǔ became the King of Wèi,
he established the positions of Secretariat Director and Assistant,
responsible for handling memorials from the Imperial Secretariat.
At the beginning of the Huángchū era,
it was changed to the Central Secretariat,
with Supervisor and Director positions established.
The Central Secretariat having a Supervisor and Director began from this time.
From Wèi through Jìn,
it became a crucial office,
what Xún Xù referred to as the "Phoenix Pond."
"Gēng"
is pronounced with the tone "gēng."
They were particularly favored and trusted,
both being additionally appointed as Palace Attendants and Grand Masters of Imperial Entertainments,
and enfeoffed as marquises of their native counties.
Fàng
was from Fāngchéng in Zhuō Commandery.
Zī,
was from Zhōngdū in Tàiyuán.
The Emperor personally attended to all affairs of state,
frequently launching military campaigns,
and the responsibilities of his most trusted confidants
were all managed by these two men;
whenever there was a major matter,
and court officials convened for discussion,
he often had them decide what was right and wrong,
selecting and implementing accordingly.
The Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎng Jì, submitted a memorial stating:
(This memorial was also submitted by Jì while serving as Central Protector;
the Comprehensive Mirror, due to narrating the affairs of Fàng and Zī, records it here.)
"Your servant has heard that when great ministers become too powerful, the state is endangered;
when those close to the ruler become too intimate, the ruler himself is obscured.
This is the ultimate warning from antiquity.
In the past, when great ministers held power,
both inside and outside the court were stirred;
(This likely refers to the time of Emperor Wén.)
Some say: It refers to the ministers who received the late emperor's testamentary decree.
None failed to be reverent and solemn.
It is not that the great ministers were not loyal,
but when authority and power lie below,
then the hearts of the multitude become disrespectful toward those above.
This is the constant tendency of such situations.
Since Your Majesty has already discerned this regarding the great ministers,
I hope you will not forget it regarding those close to you.
Those close to you may be loyal, upright, and far-sighted,
but they are not necessarily more virtuous than the great ministers.
As for being accommodating and seeking to please,
they might be quite skilled at it.
Now, what is said outside the court
often goes, 'Although those in the Central Secretariat are made to be respectful and cautious,
they dare not have external connections.'
But merely having this reputation
still confuses the common world;
how much more so when they actually grasp the crucial affairs of state,
present before Your Majesty daily?
If, taking advantage of moments of weariness, they make decisions and judgments,
(meaning, when the ruler is weary,
they make divisions and decisive judgments.)
then others will also turn toward them according to the circumstances.
Once this beginning appears,
privately recruiting allies and supporters,
assessing good and bad, slandering and praising,
will inevitably arise.
Merits, faults, rewards, and punishments
will inevitably be altered.
'Fù'
means crime;
alteration means rewards and punishments will not correspond to merits and crimes.
Those who crookedly attach themselves to those close to you will instead prosper,
entering through subtle means,
and emerging according to the situation.
Those whom Your Majesty's mind is familiar with and trusts,
you will no longer suspect or perceive.
This is something Your Sagely Wisdom should hear about early,
and outwardly show attention to state affairs,
then the boundaries of their form will naturally become apparent;
(meaning Fàng and Zī are daily by Your Majesty's side,
familiar and trusted,
and you no longer perceive their treachery;
if you do not early hear loyal words,
personally oversee all affairs,
and outwardly demonstrate attention to state matters,
then the boundaries of Fàng and Zī's form will inevitably be revealed and cannot be concealed.)
'Fù'
is pronounced 'fù.'
'Xiàn'
is pronounced 'xiàn.'
There is no one suitable to inform you.
Your servant privately believes that Your Majesty should deeply concentrate and silently ponder,
listening publicly and observing comprehensively.
If affairs are not fully in accordance with principle and things are not completely suitable for use,
then you should change the tune and adjust the melody,
aiming to rival the achievements of Huángdì and Táng Yáo in the distant past.
'Rivaling' means
matching one against the other.
Huáng and Táng refer to
Huángdì and Emperor Yáo of Táng.
How can you be limited to familiar favorites alone!
However, a ruler cannot personally handle all affairs under heaven;
he must necessarily delegate them.
If entrusted to a single minister,
unless he possesses the loyalty of a Zhōu Gōngdàn
or the impartiality of a Guǎn Yíwú,
then there will be the malady of
manipulating power and ruining the office.
Although pillars of the state are few today,
as for those whose conduct is praised in a single province,
whose wisdom is effective in a single office,
who are loyal, trustworthy, and exhaust their lives,
each fulfilling their duties,
they can all be driven and directed together,
so that this enlightened court of Your Majesty does not have the reputation of being governed by specialized officials!"
("Specialized officials"
refers to exclusively entrusting Fàng and Zī.)
Everything before this point does not pertain to this year's events.
The Comprehensive Mirror, because of Fàng and Zī's fear of losing their positions leading to their misleading the Emperor in the matter of entrusting an orphan,
thus records it here as a precursor event.
When the Emperor fell seriously ill,
he deeply pondered the matter of succession,
and therefore appointed Emperor Wǔ's son, the Prince of Yān, Cáo Yǔ, as Grand General,
along with the General of the Central Army, Xiàhóu Xiàn, and the General of the Martial Guards, Cáo Shuǎng.
(According to Wèi regulations: The General of the Central Army commanded the Central Barracks, Five Colonelcies, and Martial Guards, these three camps.)
The General of the Martial Guards
likely commanded the Martial Guards Camp.
Tàizǔ had Xǔ Chǔ in charge of the palace guard,
promoting him to General of the Household of the Martial Guards,
the title "Martial Guards" beginning from this.
Later, he was further promoted to General of the Martial Guards,
and from then on, the Martial Guards first had the title of General.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
the office of General of the Martial Guards was abolished.)
Shuǎng
was the son of Cáo Zhēn;
Zhào
was the son of Cáo Xiū.
The Emperor had been close to the Prince of Yān, Yǔ, since youth,
and therefore entrusted the matter of succession to him.
Liú Fàng and Sūn Zī had long been in charge of confidential duties,
and Xiàn and Zhào felt discontent in their hearts;
there was a chicken-roosting tree in the palace,
and the two of them said to each other:
"This too has been here a long time,
how much longer can it last!"
Chickens were kept in the palace to announce the dawn,
and they roosted in the tree,
hence it was called the chicken-roosting tree.
Xiàn and Zhào used it as a metaphor for Fàng and Zī.
With one remark, they triggered the mechanism of the Sīmǎ clan's usurpation of Wèi—
such is the importance of being careful with one's words!
From this, we can see the frivolity and rashness of Xiàn and Zhào,
how could they be entrusted with the care of an orphan!
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
Jǐ,
jū qǐ fān.
They secretly plotted to sow discord.
The Prince of Yān was by nature respectful and good,
and he sincerely and firmly declined.
The Emperor summoned Fàng and Zī into his bedchamber,
and asked:
"Is the Prince of Yān really like this?"
This means his nature is respectful and good,
and his conduct is truly like this.
"The Prince of Yān actually knows himself that he is not fit for such a great responsibility, that is all."
The Emperor said:
"Who can take on the responsibility?"
At that time, only Cáo Shuǎng was at his side,
and Fàng and Zī thus recommended Shuǎng,
and moreover said:
"It would be appropriate to summon Sīmǎ Yì to participate together."
The Emperor said:
"Is Shuǎng capable of handling the matter?"
Shuǎng broke into a sweat and could not answer.
Fàng stepped on his foot,
and whispered in his ear:
This means speaking into his ear.
"I will serve the state with my life."
The Emperor followed Fàng and Zī's words,
intending to use Shuǎng and Yì,
but then he changed his mind,
and ordered the previous command to be halted: Fàng and Zī again entered to see the Emperor and persuade him,
and the Emperor again followed them.
Fàng said:
"It would be appropriate to write a handwritten edict."
The Emperor said:
"I am extremely ill,
and cannot."
Fàng then climbed onto the bed,
took the Emperor's hand and forced him to write it,
then took it out,
and loudly announced:
"There is an edict dismissing the Prince of Yān Yǔ and others from their posts,
and they are not permitted to remain in the palace."
They all left in tears.
Examination of discrepancies: Fàng's biography says:
"Yǔ was by nature respectful and good,
and sincerely and firmly declined.
The Emperor summoned Fàng and Zī into his bedchamber,
and asked: 'Is the Prince of Yān really like this?'
Fàng and Zī replied: 'The Prince of Yān actually knows himself that he is not fit for such a great responsibility, that is all.'
The Emperor said: 'Can Cáo Shuǎng replace Yǔ?'
Fàng and Zī thus supported this.
They also strongly advised that the Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Xuānwáng should be quickly summoned,
and the Emperor accepted their words.
After Fàng and Zī left,
the Emperor changed his mind again,
and issued an edict ordering Xuānwáng not to come.
Soon after, he again saw Fàng and Zī and said: 'I myself summoned the Grand Commandant,
but Cáo Zhào and others instead made me stop him.'
He ordered another edict to be written,
and the Emperor alone summoned Shuǎng, together with Fàng and Zī, to receive the edict,
and then dismissed Yǔ, Xiàn, Zhào, and Lǎng from their posts."
According to Chén Shòu, who wrote the Records of Wèi during the Jìn era,
if he spoke of Fàng and Zī's true intentions,
it would not be considered praiseworthy at the time,
so he glossed over it and concealed it.
Now, following Xí Zàochǐ's Hàn-Jìn Spring and Autumn Annals and Guō Bān's Tales of the Generations,
it seems to capture the truth.
On the jiǎshēn day
Cáo Shuǎng was appointed as Grand General.
The Emperor considered Shuǎng's talent weak,
and additionally appointed the Imperial Secretary Sūn Lǐ as Chief Clerk to the Grand General to assist him.
This sets the stage for Shuǎng's later dismissal of Sūn Lǐ.
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
At this time,
Sīmǎ Yì was in Jí,
having just returned with his army from Liáodōng,
and was stationed at Jí.
Jí County had belonged to Hénèi Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
Pìxié,
the name of a servant,
similar to how the Hàn Chancellor's servants were called Yílù.
Previously,
the Prince of Yān had devised a plan for the Emperor,
believing that affairs in Guānzhōng were important,
and that Yì should be sent via a convenient route from Zhǐ Pass west back to Cháng'ān,
as affairs in Guānzhōng were important,
meaning preparations against Shǔ and pacifying the Dí and Qiāng.
Zhǐ County,
belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
Xián said: The old city of Zhǐ is southeast of Jìyuán County in Luò Prefecture.
The Five Dynasties Records: Zhǐ Pass,
is in Wángwū County, Hénèi Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Zhǐ Pass is within the boundaries of Jìyuán County, Hénán Prefecture.
Yì received two edicts in quick succession,
which contradicted each other,
and he suspected that there was a change in the capital,
so he hurriedly rushed to court.
1 Spring,
First Month,
Yì arrived,
entered for an audience,
and the Emperor took his hand and said:
"I entrust the future affairs to you,
you and Cáo Shuǎng shall assist the young son.
Death can be endured,
I endure death waiting for you,
to be able to meet,
I have no regrets!"
Then he summoned the Princes of Qí and Qín to show Yì,
and separately pointing to the Prince of Qí Fāng, he said to Yì:
"This is the one,
look at him carefully,
do not make a mistake!"
He also instructed the Prince of Qí to go forward and embrace Yì's neck.
Yì kowtowed and shed tears.
On this day,
the Prince of Qí was established as Crown Prince.
The Emperor soon passed away.
Chén Shòu said: He was thirty-six years old.
Péi Sōngzhī said: According to this, Cáo Cāo pacified Yè in the eighth month of the ninth year of Jiàn'ān,
and Wén Emperor first took Lady Zhēn as his consort,
so Míng Emperor should have been born in the tenth year,
counting to the first month of this year,
he was exactly thirty-four years old.
At that time, the calendar was reformed,
taking the twelfth month of the previous year as the first month of this year,
one could forcibly call it thirty-five years,
but not thirty-six.
The Emperor was deep, resolute, intelligent, and sharp,
acting according to his own will,
evaluating and selecting based on ability and achievement,
and rejecting empty falsity.
In mobilizing troops and moving masses,
deciding on major matters,
the strategists and generals
all admired the Emperor's great strategies.
He had an exceptionally strong memory,
even for the minor officials around him,
their official records, nature, and conduct,
the traces of their actions,
and their fathers, brothers, and sons,
once heard or seen,
he would never forget.
Sūn Shèng commented: I heard from the elders,
that Wèi Míng Emperor's natural appearance was outstanding,
his hair stood up and reached the ground,
he stuttered and spoke little,
but was deep, resolute, and decisive.
Initially,
when the various lords received the testament to assist and guide,
the Emperor placed them all in important positions,
meaning he sent Cáo Xiū to guard Huáinán, Cáo Zhēn to guard Guānzhōng, and Sīmǎ Yì to station at Wǎn.
Chǔ,
chāng lǚ fān.
He treated the great ministers with generous courtesy,
was open-minded and tolerant of honest advice,
even if they offended him with extreme remonstrance,
he did not destroy or kill them,
such was the greatness of his capacity as a ruler.
However, he did not think to establish virtue and leave a legacy,
nor did he solidify the foundation of the defensive walls,
the Odes say: The sons of the clan are the walls.
This means the Emperor was suspicious and jealous of the imperial clan,
leading to the downfall of Wèi.
The state had no defense,
how lamentable!
7 Guǎn Níng passed away.
Níng was renowned for his lofty and pure conduct;
people who looked up to him
felt he was distant and unattainable,
yet upon approaching him, he was amiable and easygoing.
He could guide people toward goodness through events,
and there was no one
who was not transformed and convinced.
When he died,
everyone in the realm, whether they knew him or not,
sighed in lament without exception.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Shǔ’s Jiāng Wéi led his flank army back from Hànzhōng and stationed at Fú.
At that time, all Shǔ armies were under Jiǎng Wǎn’s command,
so Jiāng Wéi only led a flank army.
2 The ruler of Wú established his son Sūn Hé as crown prince,
and issued a general pardon.
3 In the third month,
Chāngyì Jǐnghóu Mǎn Chǒng passed away.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on yǐyǒu day,
Jǐngjì, the General of the Imperial Guard, was appointed as Grand Commandant.
4 The ruler of Wú sent General Niè Yǒu and Commandant Lù Kǎi to lead thirty thousand troops to attack Dān’ěr and Zhūyá.
Dān’ěr and Zhūyá
were established as commanderies by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
belonging to Jiāozhī Province;
after Emperor Yuán, they were abandoned.
Niè
is pronounced as nièzhéfān.
Dān
is pronounced as dōugānfān.
5 In the eighth month,
the ruler of Wú enfeoffed his son Sūn Bà as Prince of Lǔ.
Bà
was the younger brother of Hé by the same mother,
and was especially favored and esteemed,
with no distinction from Hé.
This sets the stage for the later deposition of Hé and execution of Bà in Wú.
A memorial was submitted advising:
“Your subject privately believes that the Prince of Lǔ is endowed by heaven with fine virtue,
possessing both civil and military talents;
it is appropriate now
that he should guard the four directions,
serve as a bulwark for the state,
promote virtuous excellence,
and widely manifest awe-inspiring authority.
This is a sound rule for the state
and what the realm looks up to.
Moreover, the two palaces should have distinctions in status,
to rectify the order of superior and inferior,
and clarify the foundation of moral transformation.”
The memorial was submitted three or four times,
but the ruler of Wú did not heed it.
1 In spring,
the first month,

The Emperor said that Shǎokāng was born after the state's destruction,
reduced to the status of a feudal lord's servant,
yet was able to spread his virtue and initiate his plans,
ultimately destroying Guò and Gé,
restoring Yǔ's achievements,
sacrificing to Xià and matching Heaven,
not losing the old heritage.
If not for his supreme virtue and great benevolence,
how could he have accomplished such merit!
Hàn Gāozǔ relied on a collapsing situation,
wielded temporary power,
exclusively employed intelligence and force to achieve success,
his actions and conduct often violating sagely standards.
As a son, he repeatedly endangered his parents;
as a ruler, he imprisoned a worthy minister;
as a father, he could not protect his son.
After his death,
the state nearly collapsed.
If he and Shǎokāng had exchanged places in time,
he might not have been able to restore the great achievements of Yǔ.
Alas!
The Emperor indeed had the ambition of Shǎokāng,
yet he could not exterminate Jiāo and Yì and instead died by others' hands—
because he could not spread his virtue and initiate his plans.
In my view, the Emperor's discussion of the two rulers' merits and faults
was merely the talk of a bookish scholar,
unable to match the bold and forthright words of Shí Lè.

How could you think of handing over the state to others!
If there is trouble in Luòzhōng,
I will die for it.”
Chōng fell silent;
upon returning,
he reported to Zhāo:
“Zhūgě Dàn has served in Yángzhōu twice,
(Dàn previously oversaw Yángzhōu,
after the defeat at Dōngguān,
he was reassigned to oversee Yùzhōu,
and after Guànqiū Jiǎn’s death,
he resumed overseeing Yángzhōu.)
If we summon him now,
he will certainly not come,
but his rebellion will be swift and the harm small;
if we do not summon him,
his rebellion will be delayed but the harm great.
It would be better to summon him.”
Zhāo agreed.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
an edict appointed Dàn as Minister of Works,
summoning him to the capital.
Upon receiving the edict,
Dàn grew even more fearful,
suspecting that the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Lè Chēn, was slandering him,
so he killed Chēn.
(The Conquering East General and the Inspector of Yángzhōu shared governance in Shòuchūn.)
(The appointments of the Four Conquering Generals of Wèi
typically used their regional inspectors as deputy commanders,
hence Dàn suspected Chēn of slandering him.)
Jiàn,
(pronounced with the gǔxiàn tone).
(The commanderies and counties of Wèi all established military agricultural colonies,
and all those in the colonies were government soldiers.)
He gathered enough grain for a year’s supply,
planning to close the gates and defend himself.
He sent his Chief Clerk, Wú Gāng, to take his youngest son, Jìng, to Wú,
Jiàng,
(pronounced as the character).
Shào,
(pronounced with the shīzhào tone).
Jìng,
(pronounced with the jíyǐng tone,
also pronounced with the jízhèng tone).
And requested to send the sons of his subordinate officers as hostages.
(Yámén refers to the sons of various generals.)
Zhì,
(pronounced with the zhì tone).
4 The wives of Wú’s Téng Yǐn and Lǚ Jù
were both sisters of Sūnkǒu Commander Sūn Yī.
(Yī
was the son of Sūn Huàn by a concubine.)
Xià,
(pronounced with the hùyǎ tone).
Sūn Chēn sent the General Who Guards the South, Zhū Yì, to lead troops from Hǔlín to attack Yī.
When Yì reached Wǔchāng,
Yī led his troops to defect.
On the yǐsì day,
an edict appointed Yī as General of Chariots and Cavalry, Governor of Jiāozhōu,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wú,
granted him the authority to establish a personal staff and recruit officials,
ceremonial honors equal to the Three Excellencies,
a ceremonial robe and crown with red shoes,
and treated him with great generosity.
(Elevating Sūn Yī was to attract defectors.)
5 Sīmǎ Zhāo escorted the Emperor and the Empress Dowager to suppress Zhūgě Dàn.
(If Zhāo went himself,
he feared someone might later seize the two palaces and cause trouble,
so he escorted them to suppress Dàn.)
When Wú Gāng arrived in Wú,
the Wú people were greatly pleased and sent Generals Quán Yì, Quán Duān, Táng Zī, and Wáng Zuò with thirty thousand troops,
along with Wén Qīn, to rescue Dàn;
they appointed Dàn as Left Protector of the Army,
acting with imperial authority, Grand Minister over the Masses, General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shòuchūn.
(Yì was the son of Cóng;
Duān was his nephew.)
In the sixth month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xiàng,
and Sīmǎ Zhāo commanded two hundred and sixty thousand troops to advance and encamp at Qiūtóu.
(In this campaign,
Sīmǎ Zhāo renamed Qiūtóu as Wǔqiū,
to commemorate his military achievements.)
(Wǔqiū
became Shěnqiū County in the Táng dynasty.)
Together with General Who Pacifies the East, Chén Qiān, and others, they besieged Shòuchūn.
When Jī first arrived,
the encirclement of the city was not yet complete,
and Wén Qīn, Quán Yì, and others from the northeast of the city,
taking advantage of the mountains and treacherous terrain,
managed to lead their troops and break into the city.
(There were no other mountains outside Shòuchūn,
only Bāgōng Mountain to the north of the city.)
Jī repeatedly requested to advance and attack,
but at that time, Wú’s Zhū Yì led thirty thousand men to advance and encamp at Ānfēng,
providing external support for Wén Qīn.
(Ānfēng County
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and was divided into Ānfēng Commandery in the Wèi dynasty.
The current Ānfēng County is eighty lǐ south of Shòuchūn.)
Jī said to the generals:
“Now that our siege fortifications are growing stronger,
and troops are gathering,
we should only refine our defensive preparations to await their escape,
but if we shift troops to guard dangerous points,
allowing them to act freely,
even the wisest man
cannot manage the aftermath well!”
He then adhered to expediency,
and submitted a memorial:
“Now, facing the enemy,
we should stand firm as a mountain.
If we relocate to rely on dangerous terrain,
people’s hearts will waver,
greatly damaging our momentum.
All armies are positioned behind deep trenches and high ramparts,
the morale of the troops is stable,
and cannot be shaken—
this is the key to commanding troops.”
After the memorial was submitted,
he received approval.
(Approving Jī to implement his strategy.)
At that time, the Emperor was with the army,
so the command of all armies was subject to imperial directives,
but the actual decision-maker on what was permissible was Sīmǎ Zhāo.)
The defenses were doubled in layers,
and the trenches and ramparts were extremely steep.
Wén Qīn and others made several sorties to break the encirclement,
but were repelled
and driven back.
Sīmǎ Zhāo also sent the General Who Arouses Martial Spirit and Supervisor of Military Affairs in Qīngzhōu, Shí Bāo,
to oversee the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Zhōu Tài, and the Inspector of Xúzhōu, Hú Zhì, in selecting elite troops as mobile forces,
to guard against external enemies.
Tài defeated Zhū Yì at Yángyuān.
(The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jué River originates north of Yúlóu County in Lújiāng Commandery,
passes east of Ānfēng County,
then turns north,
and on the right meets the Yángquán River.
West of the river is the old city of Yángquán County,
originally Yángquán Township,
where Hàn Emperor Líng enfeoffed Huáng Wǎn as a marquis.)
The Jué River then flows north into the Huái River.
Tài pursued them,
killing and wounding two thousand men.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Great General of Wú, Sūn Chēn, dispatched a large army to station at Huòlǐ.
Later, the King of Wú reprimanded Sūn Chēn for remaining in the lake without coming ashore even a single step.
Thus, Huòlǐ must have been within the boundaries of Cháoxiàn.
Zhū Yì left the baggage and supplies at Dūlù.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Bóxiāng County,
which Wáng Mǎng renamed Yánglù,
is where the Xiè River originates.
It flows north past Sháobēi,
then turns northwest and enters the Huái River.
Could it be that Dūlù is actually Yánglù?
Furthermore, according to the Jìn Jì,
Dūlù was located south of Líjiāng.
Zhòng (重)
is pronounced with the falling tone (zhòng).
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Sháobēi Dú River flows east into the Líjiāng River.
The river flows east past the south of Líjiāng Pavilion,
then continues east to join the Féi River,
forming what is called the Líjiāng River mouth.
Tàishān Prefect Hú Liè led a surprise force of five thousand to attack Dūlù,
completely burning Zhū Yì's supplies and provisions.
Zhū Yì led his remaining troops, subsisting on kudzu leaves,
and fled back to Sūn Chēn.
Sūn Chēn ordered Zhū Yì to fight another desperate battle.
Zhū Yì, citing the lack of food for his soldiers,
did not obey Sūn Chēn's command.
Sūn Chēn was furious.
In the ninth month,
on the day Jǐsì,
Sūn Chēn beheaded Zhū Yì at Huòlǐ.
On the day Xīnwèi,
he led his troops back to Jiànyè.
The siege of Shòuchūn was already firmly established.
Even if Zhōu Yú, Lǚ Méng, and Lù Xùn were to come back to life,
they would not be able to lift it.
If Sūn Chēn could have mobilized the masses of Jīng and Yáng to march out from Xiāngyáng toward Wǎn and Luò,
the troops besieging Shòuchūn would certainly have had to divide and return to save themselves.
At that time, Zhūgě Dàn, Wén Qīn, and others could have broken through the encirclement and fought desperately,
and there might still have been a chance.
Yet he lost and destroyed his troops,
and executed his own famous general.
From this, none among the people of Wú did not resent him.
This sets the stage for Wú's later execution of Sūn Chēn.
Sīmǎ Zhāo said:
"Zhū Yì did not manage to reach Shòuchūn,
and the men of Wú killed him.
This was not his crime.
They intended to apologize to Shòuchūn and strengthen Dàn's resolve,
making him still hope for rescue.
Now we should tighten the siege,
guard against their breaking out,
and use various methods to mislead them."
He then spread disinformation,
proclaiming
"Wú's relief forces are about to arrive,
our main army is short of food,
and we are sending out the weak and sick separately to seek grain north of the Huái,
so we cannot hold out for long."
Dàn and the others consequently became more lax and ate freely.
Soon, the city ran short of grain,
and no outside relief arrived.
Generals Jiǎng Bān and Jiāo Yí,
both Dàn's trusted confidants and chief strategists,
said to Dàn:
"Zhū Yì and others came with a large force but could not advance.
Sūn Chēn killed Yì and returned to Jiāngdōng.
Outwardly, he used sending troops as a pretext,
but inwardly, he is actually sitting back waiting to see the outcome.
Xū (須)
means to wait.
Our soldiers are eager to fight.
If we combine our strength and fight a desperate battle,
attacking one side of the encirclement,
even if we cannot completely overcome them,
there are still those who might survive.
To sit idly and await death
is pointless."
This means it is better to fight desperately to seek life,
rather than sit and guard while awaiting destruction.
"You, my lord, have now entrusted over a hundred thousand troops to Wú,
and Qīn along with Quán Duān and others are all trapped together in this desperate situation.
Their fathers, brothers, sons, and grandsons are all in Jiāngbiǎo.
Even if Sūn Chēn does not wish to come,
would their sovereign and his relatives be willing to listen?
Moreover, the Central Plains have no year without troubles,
and both the army and the people are weary.
If they besiege us for a year,
internal changes will arise among them.
Why abandon this [opportunity],
to risk danger seeking a fluke victory?"
Bān and Yí persistently urged him,
angering Qīn.
Dàn wanted to kill Bān and Yí.
The two men, fearing for their lives,
in the eleventh month,
deserted Dàn, scaled the city wall, and came to surrender.
Quán Yì's nephews Huī and Yí were in Jiànyè.
Huī and Yí
were the two sons of Yì's elder brother Quán Xù.
"Huī"
is also written in one version as
"Yī".
They took their mother and led several dozen families of their troops to come and surrender.
At that time, Yì, along with his nephew Jìng and Quán Duān's younger brothers Piān and Jī, were all leading troops within the walls of Shòuchūn.
Sīmǎ Zhāo, adopting the strategy of the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Zhōng Huì,
secretly forged letters for Huī and Yí,
and had trusted associates of Huī and Yí carry them into the city to inform Yì and the others,
saying
"In Wú, they are furious with Yì and the others for being unable to relieve Shòuchūn,
meaning they are angry that Yì and the others could not extract the forces of Shòuchūn from the heavy siege.
That is why they fled and came to submit."
In the twelfth month,
Yì and the others led their several thousand troops, opened the gates, and came out to surrender.
The city was shaken with fear,
not knowing what to do.
An imperial edict appointed Yì as General Who Pacifies the East,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Línxiāng.
Duān and the others were also enfeoffed and appointed to various ranks.
6 In Hàn, Jiāng Wéi heard that Wèi had divided the Guānzhōng troops to send to Huáinán.
He wanted to take advantage of the emptiness to advance toward Qínchuān.
The land of Qín is secured by four strategic passes,
with the Wèi River flowing through its center.
On both sides of the Wèi River valley,
lie a thousand lǐ of fertile land,
which the world calls Qínchuān.
He advanced as far as Shěnlǐng.
At that time, the Great Wall stored a great amount of grain,
but had few defending troops.
General Who Conquers the West and Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Yōng and Liáng, Sīmǎ Wàng,
along with General Who Pacifies the West, Dèng Ài, advanced their troops to occupy it,
in order to resist Wéi.
Wéi fortified himself at Mángshuǐ.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Luògǔ River originates from the Luò Valley in the southeastern mountains of Méiwù.
It flows north past the west of the Great Wall,
then continues north to flow into the Wèi River.
The Wèi River flows further east,
where the Máng River comes from the south to join it.
The river originates from the Máng Valley in the southern mountains,
flows north past the bamboo garden of Zhōuzhì County,
then flows north to join the Wèi River.
I note that Luògǔ is in present-day Zhēnfú County of Yáng Prefecture.
It winds for eighty lǐ,
with a total of eighty-four bends.
Wàng and Ài did not respond.
At this time,
Jiāng Wéi repeatedly dispatched troops,
causing the people of Shǔ to suffer and grieve.
Zhōngsǎn Dàfū Qiáo Zhōu composed the "Discourse on Hostile States" to admonish him.
The Continued Records of the Hàn states: Zhōngsǎn Dàfū,
holds a salary of six hundred shí;
the Hàn Official Records state: salary equivalent to two thousand shí.
Hú Guǎng said: Guānglù Dàfū,
originally called Zhōng Dàfū,
in the fifth year of Yuánshòu under Emperor Wǔ,
the position of Jiàn Dàfū was established as Guānglù Dàfū.
During the restoration under Emperor Shìzǔ,
it was renamed Jiànyì Dàfū.
There were also Tàizhōng and Zhōngsǎn Dàfū.
These four ranks were equivalent to the lower ministers of the Son of Heaven in ancient times,
comparable to the high ministers of the feudal states.
"Someone asked: In ancient times, those who could overcome the strong despite being weak—
what was their method?
He replied: I have heard that,
those in great positions without worries often become negligent,
while those in small positions with concerns often think of improvement;
negligence leads to disorder,
while thinking of improvement leads to governance—
this is the constant principle.
Thus, King Wén of Zhōu nurtured the people,
taking much with little,
and Gōu Jiàn cared for the masses,
defeating the strong with weakness—
this was their method.
King Wén governed Qí,
starting from a territory of a hundred lǐ square,
and came to possess two-thirds of the world—
this is what is called taking much with little.
Gōu Jiàn returned to Yuè,
mourned the dead and cared for the sick,
spent ten years building up the population and resources,
and ten years educating and training,
thus using weak Yuè to defeat strong Wú.
Xiàng was strong and Hàn was weak,
and they engaged in warfare.
Xiàng Yǔ made a treaty with Hàn to divide the realm at Hónggōu,
each returning to rest their people.
Zhāng Liáng believed that the people's resolve was already settled,
and thus difficult to change,
so he led troops to pursue Yǔ,
ultimately defeating the Xiàng clan.
This event is recorded in the tenth scroll, the fourth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
He said: During the time of Shāng and Zhōu,
kings and lords were revered for generations,
meaning they held esteemed positions for generations.
The people were accustomed to this specialization;
the people were accustomed to the clear distinction between ruler and subject,
thus they were devoted to serving their superiors.
Those entrenched were difficult to move.
At that time,
even Emperor Gāo of Hàn—how could he have taken the world by wielding a sword and whipping his horse!
After Qín abolished the feudal lords and established commanderies,
meaning abolishing the feudal states and dividing them into thirty-six commanderies,
each commandery having a governor.
The world collapsed,
with some years seeing changes of rulers,
some months seeing changes of lords,
birds startled and beasts frightened,
not knowing whom to follow.
Then the powerful rose to contend,
tearing apart like tigers and wolves,
the swift and fierce gained much,
while the slow and late were devoured.
Now, both we and they have inherited states through changing dynasties.
Since this is not the turbulent end of Qín,
but a situation where six states coexist,
one can emulate King Wén,
but it is difficult to emulate Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
When the people are exhausted,
signs of unrest arise;
when superiors are negligent and inferiors violent,
the form of disintegration emerges.
A proverb says: 'Shooting recklessly and missing repeatedly,
is not as good as aiming carefully before releasing.'
Diē,
means error,
shooting repeatedly with errors and missing,
is not as good as aiming carefully before releasing.
The Book of Documents says: Like drawing a bow,
examine the arrow against the mark before releasing.
Do not change step on a whim,
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Lifting the foot is called a step.
Wéi,
pronounced yú wèi fān.
Act only after careful consideration,
thus the armies of Tāng and Wǔ did not need to fight twice to achieve victory.
Tāng attacked Jié,
one battle at Míngtiáo,
and ended the Xià mandate;
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
with one military campaign the world was greatly settled.
If one instead exhausts military force and engages in reckless campaigns,
campaigns should not be frequent,
frequency leads to recklessness.
If misfortune is encountered,
even the wise will be unable to devise a plan."
Jiāng Wéi, through repeated campaigns, brought about the downfall of Shǔ,
ultimately as Qiáo Zhōu had said.
1 Spring,
first month,
Wén Qīn said to Zhūgě Dàn:
"Jiǎng Bān and Jiāo Yí say I cannot break out and flee,
Quán Duān and Quán Yì have also led their troops to surrender,
nì,
means to welcome.
Xiáng,
pronounced hù jiāng fān.
We can still fight."
Dàn and Táng Zī and others all agreed,
so they greatly prepared siege equipment,
attacking the southern encirclement day and night for five or six days,
intending to break through the encirclement.
The armies on the encirclement walls, from high positions, launched stone-throwing carts and fire arrows,
stone-throwing carts,
are catapult carts.
Chē,
pronounced chāng zhē fān.
Arrows and stones fell like rain,
the dead and wounded covered the ground,
blood flowed filling the moats,
and they returned to the city.
Food within the city grew increasingly scarce,
and tens of thousands went out to surrender.
Qīn wanted to send out all the northerners to save food,
and hold firm with the men of Wú,
but Dàn did not agree,
leading to contention and resentment.
Qīn had long been at odds with Dàn,
only temporarily united by strategy,
and as the situation grew critical, they became more suspicious of each other.
It is said that Dàn and Qīn initially united through deceitful schemes,
and as the situation grew critical, they became more suspicious of each other.
Dàn then killed Qīn.
Qīn's sons Yāng and Hǔ led troops in a small city,
Yāng and Hǔ,
are Qīn's two sons;
at that time, Shòuchūn likely had a separate small city.
They led troops to aid him,
but the troops would not follow,
so they fled alone, climbing over the city walls,
and surrendered to Sīmǎ Zhāo.
Military officers requested their execution,
but Zhāo said:
"Qīn's crimes deserve death,
and his sons certainly deserve execution;
however, Yāng and Hǔ surrendered in desperation,
and the city has not yet fallen—
killing them would only strengthen the resolve of those inside."
So he pardoned Yāng
and Hǔ,
and had them lead several hundred cavalry to patrol the city walls,
shouting:
"Even Wén Qīn's sons are not killed—
what do the rest have to fear!"
He also petitioned to appoint Yāng and Hǔ as generals,
granting them the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Everyone inside the city was pleased,
but they grew increasingly hungry and distressed.
Sīmǎ Zhāo personally came to the encirclement,
and seeing those on the walls holding bows but not shooting,
said:
"We can attack now!"
Knowing the defenders had no will to resist.
They simultaneously beat drums and shouted, scaling the walls.
Second month,
yǐyǒu day,
they captured it.
Dàn, in dire straits,
single-handedly led his followers to break out of the small city, trying to escape,
but Sīmǎ Hú Fèn's troops attacked and killed him,
exterminating his three clans.
Several hundred of Dàn's followers,
stood with hands clasped in rows,
refusing to surrender.
Each time one was beheaded,
the others were urged to surrender,
but to the end they did not change,
until all were killed.
The history records that Zhūgě Dàn won the people's hearts,
and they died for him out of gratitude.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
"A great man receives orders from his lord,
leading troops to rescue others,
but if he cannot achieve victory,
and is instead captured by the enemy,
I cannot accept this."
So he removed his helmet and charged into the enemy formation to die.
Táng Zī, Wáng Zuò, and others all surrendered.
Táng Zī was originally from Wèi but surrendered to Wú,
see scroll seventy, sixth year of Emperor Wén's Huángchū era.
Weapons and equipment piled up like mountains.
When Sīmǎ Zhāo first besieged Shòuchūn,
Wáng Jī, Shí Bāo, and others all wanted to attack it urgently.
Sīmǎ Zhāo believed that
"Shòuchūn's walls are strong and its defenders numerous;
attacking it would certainly exhaust our strength.
If there were external enemies,
we would be attacked from both inside and out,
which is a dangerous path.
Now three rebels have gathered within this isolated city—
the three rebels
refer to Zhūgě Dàn, Wén Qīn, and Táng Zī.
I should use a comprehensive strategy to entangle them.
We will simply firmly defend on three sides.
If the Wú bandits come by land,
their army's provisions will certainly be few.
I will use mobile troops and light cavalry to cut off their supply transport;
they can be defeated without a battle.
Once the Wú bandits are defeated,
Qīn and the others will surely be captured!"
He then ordered the various armies to keep their armor on and hold their positions.
In the end, they defeated the enemy without the trouble of an assault.
Commentators also believed that
"Huáinán is still rebellious—
'still'
means one after another.
They cannot be let go;
they should all be buried in pits."
Sīmǎ Zhāo said:
"In ancient warfare,
preserving the state whole was the highest achievement,
only killing its chief villain.
This means preserving the people of that state,
only killing its ruler;
this is what is called punishing the ruler while comforting the people.
This is precisely the way to demonstrate the great magnanimity of the Central Kingdom."
Not a single person was killed.
They were distributed to the three Hé regions and nearby commanderies to settle them peacefully.
Hénán
was the capital region;
Hédōng and Hénèi were both near the capital.
'Chǔ'
is pronounced chānglǚ fān.
The remaining subordinate divine generals
were all granted temporary ranks and titles,
and the multitude was pleased and submitted.
All Huáinán officers, soldiers, officials, and commoners who were coerced or abducted by Dàn
were pardoned.
Wén Yāng and his brothers were permitted to gather their father's remains for burial,
provided with ox carts,
and sent to bury him at his old tomb.
Wén Qīn
was from Qiáo,
and his old tomb was there.
'Liàn'
is pronounced lì shàn fān.
Sīmǎ Zhāo sent a letter to Wáng Jī, saying:
"Initially, the commentators said this and that,
and many sought to relocate,
referring to the previous edict ordering the armies to shift and occupy Běishān.
It also seemed appropriate.
'Línlǚ'
means personally going to the location and inspecting the camps and fortifications.
You alone held firm to your resolve,
above defying the imperial command,
below rejecting the multitude's opinions,
ultimately achieving control over the enemy and capturing the bandits.
Even what the ancients described
could not surpass this."
Sīmǎ Zhāo wanted to send the armies' light troops deep in,
to summon and welcome the sons and younger brothers of Táng Zī and others,
taking advantage of the conflict to create a situation for destroying Wú.
Wáng Jī remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Zhūgě Kè, riding on the victory at Dōngguān,
exhausted the troops south of the Yangtze to besiege Xīnchéng.
Not only was the city not taken,
but the majority of his troops died.
The event is seen in the previous volume, the fifth year of the Shàolíng Lìgōng Jiāpíng era.
Light troops going deep in,
provisions and pay not following,
the army was destroyed at Shàngguī.
This refers to the defeat at Duàngǔ.
Both superiors and subordinates underestimated the enemy;
underestimating the enemy means plans for difficulties are not deep.
Now the bandits have recently been defeated externally,
and internal troubles are not yet quelled—
referring to the mutual suspicion between Sūn Chén and his ruler and ministers.
Moreover, the troops have been out for over a year,
and the men have thoughts of returning home.
Now we have captured one hundred thousand prisoners and taken ears,
and the guilty men have been obtained—
referring to capturing Zhūgě Dàn.
The Book of Documents says: The Duke of Zhōu resided in the east for two years,
then the guilty men were thus obtained.
There has never been a complete military victory alone as great as today's.
When Emperor Wǔ defeated Yuán Shào at Guāndù,
he himself felt what had been gained was already much,
and did not pursue the fleeing,
fearing to damage his prestige."
The event is seen in volume sixty-three, the fifth year of the Hàn Xiàndì Jiàn'ān era.
He appointed Jī as General Who Conquers the East and Commander-in-Chief of the various military affairs of Yángzhōu,
and promoted him to Marquis of Dōngwǔ.
Xí Zàochǐ said: The gentleman says that Grand General Sīmǎ in this campaign
can be said to have been able to attack with virtue.

Qiān, thinking he was going to fight,
made no preparations.
Even if Shū had indeed gone to meet the enemy in battle,

The pass city was lost,
Qiān also bore guilt for it.
Liè took advantage of the emptiness to attack the city,
Qiān fought to the death.
Qiān

'Róng'

They advanced rapidly forward,

Qí,
pronounced Qú Xī.
Jīnchéng Prefectural Governor Yáng Xīn advanced towards Gānsōng.

Qiángchuānkǒu

Xù hurried to intercept Wéi,

the tenth month,

pronounced Yù.

government office
means the government court.
Cháo,
pronounced Cháo.
Jiàn,
pronounced Xiàn.

If we proceed from Yīnpíng via bypaths through Hàn Déyángtíng
Note: The Former Hàn had no Déyáng County.

A surprise force striking at their heart,

steep and rugged,

When Dèng Ài's army reached here,

Ài wrapped himself in felt,

His officers and soldiers all climbed trees and scaled cliffs,

Jiāngyóu,

south to Miánzhōu over 200 lǐ.
Miánzhōu,

Entice,
pronounced yǒu.

Ài angrily said:

Zhōng and Zuǎn galloped back to renew the battle,

Zhān's son, Shàng, sighed:

What purpose is there in living!"
He spurred his horse, charged into the enemy formation, and died.
Dù Yòu said: In Déyáng County, Hànzhōu,
Dèng Ài defeated Zhūgé Zhān here,

Defeat,
Dèng Ài was in Chéngdū,

He said to the Shu gentry and officials:

If you had met someone like Wú Hàn,

(The incident of Wú Hàn slaughtering Chéngdū is recorded in the 42nd year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.)
"In warfare, there are those who first make a show of force and then follow with substance.

However, after such a major campaign,

Let us proceed slowly for now.
Leave twenty thousand soldiers from Lǒngyòu and twenty thousand Shu soldiers behind,
to boil salt and revive smelting,

Shu has salt wells;
Zhūtí produces silver;
Yándào and Qióngdū produce copper;
Wǔyáng, Nán'ān, Línqióng, and Miǎnyáng all produce iron.

Ài wished to restore these benefits.
Prepare for the matter of following the current downstream.
Then send envoys to inform them of the advantages and disadvantages,
and Wú will surely submit and reform.
It can be settled without a campaign.
Now we should treat Liú Shàn generously to influence Sūn Xiū,
enfeoffing Shàn as the Prince of Fúfēng,
bestowing upon him assets and wealth,
and providing for his attendants.
The commandery has the fort of Dǒng Zhuó.

Ennoble his sons as dukes and marquises,
granting them income from counties within the commandery,
to display the favor shown to those who submit to fate;
open up Guǎnglíng and Chéngyáng to await the men of Wú.

Guǎnglíng belonged to Xúzhōu,
Chéngyáng belonged to Qīngzhōu.
It seems the Wèi's Guǎnglíng commandery seat was at the old city of Huáiyīn,
and the Chéngyáng commandery seat was at Jǔ.
The territories of these two commanderies actually bordered each other.
They will follow the wind and submit!"
Zhāo sent the Army Supervisor Wèi Guàn to instruct Ài:
"Matters should be reported,
and should not be undertaken arbitrarily."
Ài reiterated, saying:
"Carrying out orders on campaign,
I have followed the strategies bestowed upon me.
The chief villain having already submitted,

I deemed it fitting and expedient.
Now Shu has submitted its masses to fate,
its lands reaching the Southern Sea.

It should be pacified and settled early.
If we wait for the state's command,
the journey back and forth on the roads,

According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
'When a great officer goes beyond the borders,

The situation is connected to Shu;

The Art of War states:
'Advancing not seeking fame,

Advancing not seeking fame,
retreating not avoiding blame.
Only protecting the people,
and benefiting the ruler,

I would never, out of personal suspicion, damage the state's plans!"
Zhōng Huì harbored rebellious intentions within.
Jiāng Wéi knew this,

"I have heard that since your time in Huáinán,

(Shuì,

"Your words are far-reaching,

(Meaning to rebel.)

First year of Xiánxī
(Jiǎshēn, 264 AD) (In the fifth month of this year,

first month,

oiled,

escort without axe carriages.
Near small envoy carriages,
orchid carriages, red hubs,
white canopies, red curtains,
followed by forty outriders.
These were used for pursuit, arrest, investigation,
and for those on special missions.
Various envoy carriages,
all had vermilion-spoked wheels,
four spokes,
red yokes.
Ài was still lying in bed, not yet risen,
so they arrested Ài and his son,
placing Ài in a cage cart.
The generals plotted to rescue Ài,
arming themselves and rushing to Guàn's camp;
Guàn lightly went out to meet them,
pretending to have drafted a memorial,
intending to clarify Ài's case,
falsely claiming he would explain that Ài had no rebellious intent.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Zhōng Huì arrived at Chéngdū,
and sent Dèng Ài to the capital.
Huì only feared Ài,
and now that Ài and his son were captured,
Huì alone commanded the great army,
his authority shaking the western lands.
He thus resolved to plot rebellion.
Huì wanted to have Jiāng Wéi lead fifty thousand men out through Xiégǔ as the vanguard,
while he himself would follow with the main army.
Once they reached Cháng'ān,
he would order the cavalry to take the land route and the infantry the water route,
floating down the Wèi River with the current into the Huáng Hé,
believing they could reach Mèngjīn in five days,
join forces with the cavalry at Luòyáng,
and in a single day, the empire could be settled.
Easier said than done!
"I fear Dèng Ài might not submit to the summons,
so I now dispatch Central Protector of the Army Jiǎ Chōng to lead ten thousand infantry and cavalry directly into Xiégǔ,
to station at Lèchéng,
the Lèchéng fortified by Zhūgě Liàng at Chénggù.
We shall meet soon."
Huì, receiving the letter, was alarmed.
He called his close associates and told them:
"Merely capturing Dèng Ài,
the Imperial Chancellor knows I can handle alone;
meaning Sīmǎ Zhāo knew Huì was fully capable of handling the capture of Ài.
Yǔ,
niú jù fān.
He must now realize I am different,
different,
meaning changed.
If the affair succeeds,
we can gain the empire;
if it fails,
we retreat to defend Shǔ and Hàn,
not failing to become another Liú Bèi!"
Shǔ, Hàn,
refers to the lands of the Shǔ and Hànzhōng commanderies of Hàn.
On the dīngchǒu day,
Huì summoned all the Protectors of the Army, commandery governors, Yámén cavalry commanders and above
—these were all those with Huì's army in Chéngdū—
to hold mourning for the Empress Dowager in the Shǔ court hall,
(clarifying that Empress Dowager Guō of the Míngyuán era passed away last year).
The Shǔ capital Chéngdū had a court hall.
Cháo,
zhí yáo fān.
He had them rise in arms to depose Sīmǎ Zhāo,
all displayed the order to those seated,
had them discuss below, and when finished,
wrote it on tablets and appointed officials,
further having his trusted men take command of the various armies;
the summoned officials,
he confined them all in the various offices of Yìzhōu,
the city gates and palace gates were all closed,
with strict guards surrounding and guarding them.
Wèi Guàn feigned critical illness,
and went out to the outer offices.
Huì believed him,
and had nothing more to fear.
Jiāng Wéi wanted Huì to kill all the northern generals,
then he himself would kill Huì,
bury all the Wèi soldiers,
and re-establish the Hàn sovereign.
He secretly wrote to Liú Shàn, saying:
"I hope Your Majesty endures a few days of humiliation,
your servant wishes to make the altars of state imperiled yet restored to safety,
the sun and moon darkened yet restored to brightness."
Jiāng Wéi's heart,
was for Hàn from beginning to end.
A thousand years hence,
it shines brightly like cinnabar.

was loved and trusted by Huì.

Liè deceived his personal soldier and secretly wrote to his son Yuān, saying:

Huì has already prepared a great pit,
several thousand white clubs,

kā,

On the jǐmǎo day,
at midday,

The various armies, without prior arrangement, all clamored and came out,
with no one urging them on,
yet they vied to be first to reach the city.
At that time, Huì was just issuing armor and weapons to Jiāng Wéi,
when it was reported there was a clamorous noise outside,
like a fire,
and after a while,
it was reported soldiers were running toward the city.
Huì was alarmed,
and said to Wéi:

what should we do?"
Wéi said:
"We should just attack them!"
Huì sent soldiers to kill all the confined Yámén commanders and commandery governors,
the confined men together lifted tables to barricade the door,
(confined men,

Jī,
jǔ qǐ fān,

outside the city, they leaned ladders to climb the walls,
sī,
means this;
xū,

meaning not much time in between,

arrows fell like rain,

Jiāng Wéi led Huì's attendants in battle,

the multitude fought and beheaded Wéi,

Examination of discrepancies: The biography of Wèi Guàn says:

held it up to show Guàn,

saw Hú Liè's former attendant,
had him announce to the three armies,

Huì pressured Guàn to decide,
they stayed up all night without sleeping,
each with a sword laid across their knees.
The various armies outside had already secretly planned to attack Huì,
but since Guàn did not come out,
they did not dare act first.
Huì sent Guàn to console and reward the armies,
Guàn then went down from the hall.
Huì regretted sending him,

Guàn pleaded dizziness from his illness acting up,
feigned collapse to the ground;
by the time he left the pavilion,
several tens of messengers pursued him.
Guàn reached the outer offices,
drank salt water,

It says
"Sīmǎ Yì held the weighty position of a senior general,
and his sons all possessed great talent and bold strategy.
The Empress knew the Emperor was not a loyal subject of Wei,
and since she herself was a niece of the Wei house,
the Emperor deeply feared her,
and thus she died by poison."
At that time, Sīmǎ Yì was trusted by Emperor Míng,
and there were no signs of disloyalty,
let alone from his sons!
Merely because she was a Wei niece,
he would poison his wife?
This is entirely not factual,
but rather exaggerated rhetoric.
Otherwise,
Sīmǎ Shī himself poisoned her for some other reason.
It is not adopted here.
